en: sentence-final softener: friendly reminder, mild surprise, "oh"

example.en: Remember to bring an umbrella tomorrow, okay?

note: Turns statements into friendly reminders; Taiwan uses it far more than the mainland. 好喔 = cheerful okay. As a one-word reply, a flat 喔 sounds cold or uninterested.

example.en: It's fine, really, I'll do it myself.

note: Adds push: reassuring (沒事啦), insisting (真的啦) or impatient (快點啦). 好啦 = fine, I give in; compare 好喔 (happy yes) and 好吧 (reluctant).

en: sentence-final: mild surprise or emphasis, "hey, actually"

example.zh: 這部電影真的很好看耶。
example.en: Hey, this movie is actually really good.

note: Flags something as noteworthy or unexpected: 不錯耶; 我不知道耶 softens "I don't know". Said alone as yē it means "yay!". Mainland speakers rarely end sentences this way.

example.en: Hey, are you free in a bit?

note: Opening 欸 grabs a friend's attention (for strangers use 不好意思). Sentence-final 欸 (你很煩欸) adds exasperation or emphasis, like 耶 but blunter.

example.en: It's really hot today, huh.

note: From Taiwanese honnh. Seeks agreement the speaker already expects; softer than 對不對. Sentence-initial 齁 is an exasperated "ugh". Also written 吼 or 厚.

example.en: Ugh, how are you late again!

note: Same Taiwanese honnh as 齁, usually spelled 吼 when it opens a complaint. Whiny-annoyed rather than truly angry; often cute or flirty between friends.

example.en: What about mine? Did you get me one?

note: Colloquial 呢, from Taiwanese --leh. X咧? = "where is / what about X?". In retorts (我才不要咧, 不然咧) it sounds cheeky. More casual than 呢.

example.en: I told you so, didn't I.

note: Marks something as self-evident (本來就是嘛) or coaxes (去嘛). Shared with the mainland, but Taiwan pairs it with a whiny 撒嬌 tone: 好嘛～ = "pretty please".

example.en: Huh? What did you just say?

note: The default Taiwanese "huh?". Mainlanders hear it as rude, but in Taiwan it is neutral among peers. With elders or customers say 不好意思，你說什麼？ A long 蛤～ = "whaat, no way".

en: oh? (realization or doubt); softer variant of 喔

example.en: Oh? So he's your classmate.

note: Rising 哦？ = "oh really?" with interest or doubt; falling 哦 = "I see". As a final particle it is interchangeable with 喔 in texting; 喔 is the commoner spelling in Taiwan.

en: sentence-final: cheerful "now then; here we go"

example.en: I'm heading off now, bye!

note: A brighter 了 that announces something lightly (開動囉, 下班囉). Friendly and upbeat; shop staff use it constantly. 好了 states a fact, 好囉 chirps it.

en: oh my; ouch; "well, look at you"

example.en: Well well, not bad!

note: All-purpose reaction: pain, surprise, teasing admiration (哎唷，不錯喔 is a Jay Chou catchphrase) or playful embarrassment. Also written 唉唷, 哎喲.

example.en: Oh really, I had no idea.

note: The default "oh yeah?" backchannel. Lively tone = interested; flat tone = "I don't care", a known conversation killer. Mainland 是吗 questions; 是喔 mostly just acknowledges.

example.en: Yeah, I think it's expensive too.

note: The most common way to agree. 對啊 = "yes, I think so too"; 對齁 = "oh right, I forgot"; 對呀 is softer. Mainland-style 是的/是啊 sound stiff in Taiwan.

example.en: Oh right, it's closed on Mondays.

note: Said when reminded of something you forgot or had not considered. 對啊 agrees with what you already thought; 對齁 concedes "you're right, it slipped my mind". Also 對吼, 對厚.

example.en: Yes, yes, that's the place!

note: A rapid triple 對 shows you are following and strongly agree. Said flatly or too often, it sounds like you are brushing the person off.

example.en: For real? They broke up?

note: Clipped 真的假的, very common among under-40s. Expresses surprise more than doubt; no answer needed. Too casual for bosses or elders: say 真的嗎.

en: okay, fine (giving in); all right already

example.en: Okay, fine, I'll go with you.

note: Agreeing after some resistance, or wrapping up a topic (好啦，先這樣). 好喔 = glad yes, 好吧 = reluctant, 好啦 = "fine, you win". A sharp tone makes it "enough already".

example.en: Sure, I'll be there at six then.

note: Friendly, compliant yes; the texting default. Warmer than 好, less formal than 好的. 好啦 concedes, 好吧 is unenthusiastic. A lone 喔 as a reply is much colder.

example.en: Okay then, let's do it another time.

note: Shared with the mainland; listed for contrast. 好吧 accepts with a hint of disappointment, 好啦 gives in, 好喔 is happy. A texted 好吧 can read as slightly hurt.

example.en: Anything's fine with me, makes no difference.

note: "Either way is fine." Neutral when choosing between options, but about someone's feelings or effort (沒差啦) it can sound indifferent or sulky.

example.en: "Is it very spicy?" "Not really."

note: As an answer it usually means "not very", a polite downplay: 還好 to 累嗎？ = not that tired. A flat 還好吧 deflates praise. Sentence-initial 還好 = "luckily".

example.en: "Thank you!" "No problem."

note: The everyday Taiwanese reply to thanks, short for "it's no trouble". 不客氣 sounds more formal or textbook. Mainlanders may misread it as "I can't". Also answers an apology.

en: it's fine; never mind; no worries

example.en: It's nothing, you go ahead with your stuff.

note: Dismisses an apology, a worry or your own aborted remark. 沒事啦 is warmer. Careful: 你沒事吧 shows concern, but 你有事嗎 is slang for "what's wrong with you?".

example.en: Mm-hm, got it.

note: Doubled to sound engaged and friendly, in chat and in speech. A single 嗯 can read as curt and 嗯哼 as smug. Typed with zhuyin ㄣ.

example.en: Ohh, so that's how it is.

note: Doubling makes 喔 sound attentive instead of cold. 喔喔 = "ah, got it"; a single 喔 as a whole reply risks sounding annoyed.

en: oh, I see; is that so

example.en: Oh I see, let me think it over then.

note: Neutral acknowledgment that buys thinking time; it neither agrees nor disagrees. 是喔 reacts to news, 這樣喔 reacts to an explanation. Also 這樣啊.

example.en: Huh, where's my phone?

note: For noticing something odd. 咦 = puzzled, 蛤 = didn't catch it or can't believe it, 欸 = hey. Shared with the mainland but far more frequent in Taiwanese speech and texting.

en: annoying, difficult, a pain (of a person)

example.en: Our manager is a real pain.

note: Literally "scooter"; a euphemism for the vulgar 雞歪. Means petty, obstructive, hard to deal with. Mild enough among friends, but not to someone's face.

example.en: He's really fussy about details.

note: From Taiwanese ku-moo. Overly particular and slow to decide. Mildly negative, but also a common self-description: 我比較龜毛.

example.en: You're so tactless, she just broke up.

note: From Taiwanese pe̍h-ba̍k "white eyes": someone who obliviously says or does the wrong thing. Teasing among friends, an insult otherwise.

example.en: A two-hour line? That's insane.

note: The current go-to for "that's crazy": 很扯, 超扯, 太扯了, for prices, stories and behavior. Medium strength, fine in any informal setting.

example.en: He actually stood me up. Unbelievable.

note: Used as a stand-alone reaction. The 2017 meme form is 傻眼貓咪. Mainland 傻眼 exists but is not a constant filler reaction as in Taiwan.

example.zh: 他這樣講我真的很無言。
example.en: When he says things like that I'm just speechless.

note: Taiwan says 無言 where the mainland says 无语. Signals exasperation rather than shock: 我無言了.

en: damn!; to bitch and moan; "as hell"

example.en: Damn, I forgot my wallet!

note: From Taiwanese khàu-pē "cry for one's father". Mid-strength swear: everyday among friends, rude to elders or at work. Also a verb (不要再靠北了) and intensifier (靠北貴).

example.zh: 你不要一直靠腰好不好？
example.en: Can you stop griping all the time?

note: From Taiwanese khàu-iau "cry from hunger". Used like 靠北 and felt as a notch milder. Softer spellings: 靠夭, 靠邀.

example.en: Damn, my EasyCard is gone.

note: Truncated 靠北 and the mildest of the family; 哇靠 = "holy crap". Still not for elders, teachers or customers.

example.en: F***, I cracked my phone screen again.

note: The strongest everyday swear. Among close male friends it is a casual exclamation; aimed at a person or shouted in public it is truly offensive. Online often written 淦.

example.zh: 我比較雞婆，提醒你一下。
example.en: I'm a bit of a busybody, so just a reminder.

note: From Taiwanese ke-pô. Milder than English "nosy" and often self-deprecating before unasked-for help. 不要那麼雞婆 = mind your own business.

example.zh: 今天遇到一個奧客，氣死。
example.en: Got a nightmare customer today, so mad.

note: From Taiwanese àu-kheh "rotten customer". Every service worker's word. 奧 alone also means lousy (奧步 = dirty trick).

example.en: My friend stood me up yesterday.

note: Shared with the mainland but used constantly in Taiwan, usually as 放我鴿子 or 被放鴿子. A last-minute cancellation by text counts too.

example.en: Stop pestering me, I'm not going.

note: From Taiwanese lôo. 很盧 = won't take no for an answer; 盧小小 is the playful, crude-origin intensifier. Kids 盧 their parents, exes 盧 their exes.

en: all talk; to trash-talk; hot air

example.en: He's all talk and never does anything.

note: Talking big without action, or trash-talking for fun (互相嘴砲). 嘴 alone is a verb: 很會嘴, 被嘴. Casual and slightly crude.

en: to shoot down (an idea, a person)

example.zh: 我的提案又被老闆打槍。
example.en: My proposal got shot down by the boss again.

note: Being rejected: proposals at work, confessions in love. Careful: it is also crude slang for male masturbation, so context matters.

en: to poke fun at, to roast, to call out

example.en: My friends love roasting me.

note: From Taiwanese thuh-tshàu; reached the mainland via anime subtitles. Taiwan often says tù cáo and mostly means teasing a person, not ranting in general.

example.zh: 樓下那幾個屁孩又在吵。
example.en: Those brats downstairs are making a racket again.

note: Also 小屁孩. Annoying kids or teens, and adults who act like them (online gamers especially). Mildly rude; said about people, not to their parents.

example.zh: 我週末都很宅，不想出門。
example.en: I'm a homebody on weekends, I don't want to go out.

note: From Japanese otaku via PTT. In Taiwan 宅 keeps a nerdy-guy flavor (宅男, 阿宅) and is often self-mockery. 宅在家 = hole up at home.

example.en: She talks in such a fake way.

note: From Taiwanese ké-pai. Acting cute, refined or humble in a fake way. Stronger and more colloquial than 做作. Often said about influencers.

example.en: Good thing I brought an umbrella.

note: Sentence-opening "thank goodness"; can also stand alone as "phew!". Mainland speech prefers 幸好 or 还好.

example.en: The beef noodles here are great.

note: From Taiwanese tsán. Everyday praise for food, ideas and plans. 按讚 = to like a post. On the mainland 棒 fills the adjective role.

example.en: It's super hot today.

note: The default intensifier for under-50s: 超好吃, 超累, often with a final 的. The mainland has 超 too but leans on 特别, 贼, 巨.

en: extremely, to the max (suffix or prefix)

example.en: I'm completely wiped out today.

note: Attaches after adjectives: 累爆, 貴爆, 好吃到爆. Before a verb it means "massively": 爆哭, 爆睡. Young and casual.

example.en: It's so damn hot today.

note: From Taiwanese ū-kàu. Adds a grumbling or emphatic feel, usually with negatives (有夠扯, 有夠貴). More local-sounding than 超.

example.en: This movie is pretty good.

note: Taiwan's "pretty / quite", usually 蠻…的; also written 滿. Mainland speech uses 挺…的. Often a polite understatement for "very".

example.en: You dummy, the door wasn't even locked.

note: Taiwanese pe̍h-tshi (白痴) spelled by sound; the number form is 87. A friendly insult among peers, a real one to strangers.

example.en: Yeah right, as if you get up that early.

note: Calls out an exaggeration among friends. Crude but light. The longer form is 聽你在屁.

en: to BS, to make stuff up; bullshit

example.en: Cut the BS, who'd believe that.

note: From Taiwanese hóo-lān; crude in origin but mild today. Tall tales and excuses. Works as verb or noun (都在唬爛). Also written 虎爛.

example.zh: 我今天很廢，什麼都沒做。
example.en: I was useless today, got nothing done.

note: 廢 covers "useless" (這功能很廢) and "being a slug" (耍廢, 廢了一整天). Mostly self-mocking.

example.en: It's unbelievably hot today.

note: Adjective + 到不行, positive or negative (累到不行). A Taiwan pattern; the mainland says 得不行.

example.zh: 昨天演唱會大家都很嗨。
example.en: Everyone was so hyped at the concert yesterday.

note: From English "high": 很嗨, 嗨起來, 嗨翻. Also the greeting "hi". Older spelling: high.

example.en: This café is really chill.

note: A youth staple since about 2018, spread by Taiwanese hip-hop. For places, people and plans: 來去chill一下.

en: to snap at, to diss, to talk back

example.zh: 他直接嗆老闆，大家都嚇到。
example.en: He snapped right back at the boss and everyone was shocked.

note: From Taiwanese tshiàng-siann (嗆聲). 被嗆 = get told off; 很嗆 = sassy, in-your-face. The mainland equivalent is 怼.

en: to make snide remarks, to mock sarcastically

example.en: He's always snide, just ignore him.

note: 酸人 = throw shade; 被酸 = get mocked; online haters are 酸民. 講話酸酸的 = passive-aggressive.

example.zh: 你有事嗎？幹嘛突然大叫。
example.en: What's wrong with you? Why'd you suddenly yell?

note: Since about 2015, 你有事嗎 or 你很有事 = "are you okay in the head?". Teasing among friends. The literal sense "to have something on" is unchanged.

en: to overwork or stay up until wrecked

example.zh: 為了趕報告，我爆肝三天。
example.en: I wrecked myself for three days to finish the report.

note: "Exploding liver": Taiwanese folk wisdom links late nights to liver damage. Students, engineers and gamers all 爆肝.

example.en: I skipped class today to see a movie.

note: Taiwan says 翹課, 翹班 (skip work), 翹掉; the mainland says 逃课, 旷工. Also written 蹺課.

example.en: I failed calculus.

note: From 當掉. A professor who fails many 很會當人. The mainland says 挂科. Fourth tone: dàng.

example.en: I'm new here, please go easy on me.

note: From Taiwan army slang; the veteran is 老鳥. 很菜 = green, inexperienced. Spread to the mainland in the 1990s.

example.en: This lunchbox place is great value.

note: Used by everyone for food, phones, flights. CP值高 = great deal. The mainland says 性价比. Not to be confused with CP = fan "couple".

en: to go for it; to rush to (a place, a sale)

example.en: The anniversary sale is tomorrow, wanna go for it?

note: 衝了 = "I'm in, let's go"; 衝一波 = go all in. Also 夜衝 = spontaneous late-night ride.

example.en: It's getting late, I'm gonna take off.

note: A casual exit line; 我先閃 for short. Friendly, never formal. 閃 also means dodge: 閃開！

example.en: Your girlfriend is really pretty.

note: The standard casual compliment for a pretty woman: 很正, 超正, 正妹. Guys say it most, but women use it about other women too. For men say 帥.

example.zh: 他上班偷看影片被抓包。
example.en: He got caught watching videos at work.

note: From Taiwanese lia̍h-pau. Mostly passive: 被抓包. For lies, cheating and slacking.

en: to screw up, to have a mishap

example.zh: 這次活動千萬不能出包。
example.en: We absolutely can't have a screw-up at this event.

note: Mistakes at work or at events: 又出包了. Milder than 搞砸. 凸槌 is the Taiwanese-flavored synonym.

en: to nag, to mutter on and on

example.en: My mom nags on and on every day.

note: Modeled on Taiwanese. Parents and partners do it; it also covers muttering to yourself. 被念 = get nagged.

example.zh: 一碗麵三百塊，太誇張了。
example.en: Three hundred NT for a bowl of noodles is outrageous.

note: In Taiwan a constant verdict on prices, behavior and news: 很誇張, 誇張欸. The mainland uses 夸张 more literally (exaggerated).

example.en: He's had a sour face on since morning.

note: 擺臭臉 = to sulk visibly. 臭臉店員 is a classic complaint in restaurant reviews.

en: to zone out, to empty one's mind

example.en: I just want to go to the beach and zone out.

note: Positive in Taiwan: deliberate mental rest (放空一下). Staring blankly in a meeting is also 放空.

example.en: Sorry, I'm late.

note: From Taiwanese pháinn-sè; also written 拍謝. Softer and friendlier than 對不起; covers "sorry", "excuse me" and sheepish thanks. Fine with strangers, too casual for formal writing.

example.en: My grandma raised me from when I was little.

note: Taiwanese a-má. Used by nearly everyone instead of 奶奶 or 外婆, and for any elderly woman (隔壁阿嬤). 阿媽 is an older spelling.

example.zh: 阿公每天早上去公園運動。
example.en: Grandpa exercises in the park every morning.

note: Taiwanese a-kong. The normal word in most families whether or not they speak Taiwanese; also used for any elderly man.

en: older man, "uncle" (a man of one's parents' age or older)

example.en: That old guy is selling roasted sweet potatoes.

note: Taiwanese a-peh. A friendly way to refer to or address an older working-class man. To his face it is fine if he is clearly over 60; otherwise 大哥 is safer.

en: a good deal, a perk, freebies

example.en: Let me know if there's a good deal.

note: From Taiwanese hó-khang. Everywhere in marketing: 好康優惠, 好康報你知. Also "lucky break": 哪有這麼好康的事.

example.en: What the hell are you saying? I don't get it.

note: Taiwanese siánn-siâu (siâu = semen). Crude: normal banter between close male friends, hostile to anyone else. Softer spellings: 殺小, 啥小. Never use it upward.

example.en: Drunk driving is a real no-no.

note: Taiwanese m̄-thang "must not", respelled as "mother soup". A 2018 streamer meme that stuck. Jokey; for a serious prohibition say 不行.

en: to talk nonsense, to say things irresponsibly

example.en: Don't go talking nonsense.

note: Taiwanese oo-pe̍h-kóng; 黑白 (oo-pe̍h) = recklessly, at random. Mild: "don't just say whatever". The Mandarin version is 亂講.

example.en: The three-pointer's in. Beautiful!

note: Taiwanese suí--lah (媠 "beautiful"). A cheer for a good play or good news. 水 alone = pretty.

example.en: We're off tomorrow? Awesome!

note: Taiwanese tsán--lah. Hearty approval, more local than 太好了. Thumbs-up energy at any age.

en: to invite along, to round people up

example.en: Remember to invite me to the next dinner.

note: From Taiwanese tsio (招). The everyday verb for getting people together. 不揪 = "you didn't invite me!", the standard jokey complaint.

en: to get a group together (outing or group buy)

example.en: Let's get a group together and go camping.

note: 揪 + 團. For trips, meals and group purchases (團購). Very common in LINE groups and on social media.

en: to sort out, to negotiate, to adjust

example.en: I'll work out the time with him.

note: From Taiwanese tshiâu (撨). 喬時間, 喬位子, 喬事情. In politics 喬 implies backroom deals. Indispensable at work.

en: to shoot the breeze, to talk rubbish

example.zh: 我們只是在喇賽，沒講正事。
example.en: We were just shooting the breeze, nothing serious.

note: Taiwanese lā-sái, literally "stir shit", but mild in use: aimless chat among friends. Because of the crude origin, avoid it in formal settings.

example.en: Good lord, these noodles are way too spicy.

note: Taiwanese iáu-siū "die young", originally a curse. Now an exclamation and intensifier (夭壽貴, 夭壽好吃). Older people may still find it coarse.

en: to wander around, to be out and about

example.zh: 颱風天不要出去趴趴走。
example.en: Don't go wandering around on a typhoon day.

note: Taiwanese pha-pha-tsáu. Light and friendly; used in travel shows and by parents scolding kids who are never home.

example.zh: 不敢去告白？你很俗辣欸。
example.en: Too scared to confess? You're such a wimp.

note: From Taiwanese tsut-á (卒仔 "pawn"). Teasing among friends for backing down; fighting talk between strangers.

en: very Taiwanese in style (local, earthy, unpolished)

example.zh: 他穿藍白拖去上課，很台。
example.en: He wears blue-and-white flip-flops to class. So Taiwanese.

note: Once a put-down for unsophisticated local taste, now often proud or affectionate (台味). Tone decides. From a foreigner, 你很台 is risky.

example.en: He's working hard to make it on his own, far from home.

note: Taiwanese phah-piànn; also written 打拚. The Taiwanese work ethic in one word (愛拚才會贏). Fully at home in Mandarin.

en: the fine points, tricks of the trade

example.en: There are a lot of fine points to this job.

note: Taiwanese mê-kak (鋩角). The subtle know-how and unwritten rules you only learn by doing. Very common office vocabulary.

example.en: Thank goodness I saved the file first.

note: Taiwanese hó-ka-tsài (好佳哉). Same slot as 好險 or 還好, with a relieved, folksy ring.

en: to go berserk, to freak out

example.zh: 電腦一直當機，我快抓狂了。
example.en: My computer keeps freezing and I'm about to lose it.

note: A Mandarin calque of Taiwanese lia̍h-kông that became standard usage and spread to the mainland through Taiwanese TV.

en: to make excuses and blame others

example.zh: 自己遲到不要牽拖別人。
example.en: Don't blame others when you're the one who's late.

note: Taiwanese khan-thua. Dragging in unrelated people or reasons to dodge responsibility. 很會牽拖 is a common complaint.

example.en: He wins once and gets all cocky.

note: Taiwanese tshàu-phuì. Lighter than 囂張; often said with a grin about a friend who is showing off.

example.zh: 要付錢的時候他就落跑了。
example.en: He ran off right when it was time to pay.

note: Taiwanese làu-pháu; many people say lào pǎo in Mandarin. 落跑新娘 = runaway bride. Casual; common in news headlines.

example.zh: 這次請到很多大咖來演講。
example.en: They got a lot of big names to speak this time.

note: Taiwanese tuā-kha (大跤). 咖 "player" also gives 小咖 (small fry), 怪咖 (weirdo), A咖 (A-lister). Spread to the mainland via variety shows.

example.en: I'm really grateful for your help this time.

note: As a thank-you it follows Taiwanese kám-un and Buddhist-group usage (感恩喔). Warmer than 謝謝; 感恩啦 is a hearty "thanks, man".

en: to worship, to make offerings at a temple or altar

example.zh: 初一十五我媽都會去拜拜。
example.en: My mom goes to worship on the 1st and 15th of every lunar month.

note: Taiwanese pài-pài. Said bài bài with full fourth tones; "bye-bye" is bāi bāi, written 掰掰. A core part of daily life.

en: to go on to the next venue (after dinner or drinks)

example.zh: 聚餐結束要不要去續攤？
example.en: Want to go on somewhere else after the dinner?

note: Taiwanese suà-thuann. A second round at a bar, KTV or late-night food stall. Essential social vocabulary.

example.zh: 中午要不要一起訂便當？
example.en: Want to order lunchboxes together at noon?

note: From Japanese bentō through Taiwanese piān-tong, a colonial-era loan. Everyday life: 鐵路便當, 排骨便當. 領便當 = (a character) gets killed off.

example.zh: 我今天很衰，出門就下雨。
example.en: I'm so unlucky today; it rained the moment I stepped out.

note: From Taiwanese sue. 衰 = bad luck: 衰爆, 帶衰 (to jinx), 衰尾. Everyday and harmless.

example.en: The netizens tore this story apart.

note: Originally PTT users, from a Stephen Chow film line about villagers gathering to gawk; now any Taiwanese netizen. 鄉民的正義 = online mob justice.

example.zh: 我這個肥宅週末只想打電動。
example.en: A fat nerd like me just wants to game all weekend.

note: PTT self-deprecation that went mainstream; mostly men about themselves. 肥宅快樂水 = cola. Insulting if aimed at a stranger.

example.en: The ramen here is great, recommended!

note: PTT comments are 推 (upvote), 噓 (boo) or → (neutral); 推爆 = 100 upvotes. In speech 推 or 大推 means "I recommend it". Mainland forums say 顶.

example.en: Did the OP ever post an update?

note: From "original post(er)"; also written 原PO. PO文 = to post, PO上網 = put online. The normal term on PTT, Dcard and Facebook.

en: to show off one's relationship (PDA, couple posts)

example.en: They flaunt their relationship in their stories every day.

note: "Emit flashes" that blind singles; the reaction is 閃瞎 or 好閃. Light teasing, never truly negative. The mainland says 秀恩爱.

example.zh: 遲到一小時還罵我，是在哈囉？
example.en: An hour late and he yells at me? What the heck?

note: Went viral around 2018–2019 among students. Mocks behavior that makes no sense: 你是在哈囉？ Casual and cheeky; now ordinary young speech.

example.en: A wage slave's daily life is overtime.

note: From Japanese shachiku "company livestock". A self-mocking label for office workers. The mainland also says 打工人.

example.en: Monday mornings make me especially sick of life.

note: A 2016–2017 buzzword (厭世代) for burnt-out young people. Used lightly: 厭世臉 = deadpan resting face. The mainland equivalent is 丧.

example.zh: 下班喝一杯珍奶是我的小確幸。
example.en: A bubble tea after work is my little bit of happiness.

note: From Haruki Murakami; hugely popular in 2010s Taiwan, later criticized as a low-ambition mindset. Still everyday vocabulary.

en: to laze around and do nothing

example.en: On my days off I just want to laze around at home.

note: Proudly unproductive resting, no shame attached. The standard word for a lazy weekend. Mainland 摆烂 is more negative.

example.en: He's left me on read for three days.

note: LINE shows 已讀 under seen messages, so the word became a verb: 已讀我 = saw it and did not answer. Central to Taiwanese dating talk.

example.zh: 他每次都已讀不回，很沒禮貌。
example.en: He always leaves me on read. So rude.

note: The classic LINE grievance. 不讀不回 is colder still; the joke form 已讀亂回 means replying with nonsense.

en: to flood a feed or chat with posts

example.zh: 我的臉書被選舉新聞洗版。
example.en: My Facebook is flooded with election news.

note: Filling the board (版) so that everything else is pushed off. The mainland says 刷屏. Also written 洗板.

example.zh: 有沒有這次颱風的懶人包？
example.en: Is there a quick explainer for this typhoon?

note: "Lazy person's pack": a digest of a complicated news story, from PTT. Now used by media and government agencies alike.

example.zh: 這支影片一看就是業配。
example.en: This video is obviously sponsored.

note: Short for 業務配合. 業配文 = advertorial; 接業配 = take a sponsorship. The mainland says 软广 or 恰饭.

example.zh: 我昨天拍了新手機的開箱。
example.en: I shot an unboxing of my new phone yesterday.

note: Took off on Taiwanese forums like Mobile01. Extended to anything shown for the first time: 開箱新家, 開箱飯店.

en: to hit a dud (bad restaurant, purchase, show)

example.zh: 這家餐廳評價很高，結果踩雷。
example.en: This restaurant had great reviews, but it was a dud.

note: "Step on a mine". Reviews promise to help you 避雷. Not about spoilers; that is 被雷 or 爆雷.

example.zh: 這篇有雷，還沒看的不要點。
example.en: This post has spoilers; don't click if you haven't watched it.

note: Two senses: spoiler (有雷, 防雷, 被雷到) and "bad, a liability" (很雷, 雷隊友, 雷包). Both everyday.

example.zh: 你不要爆雷，我還沒看完。
example.en: No spoilers, I haven't finished it yet.

note: The Taiwan word for spoiling; 劇透 is also understood. On the mainland 爆雷 means a financial product blowing up: a false friend.

example.en: This boy band is really good-looking.

note: From Japanese via the mainland; fully naturalized. 高顏值 is applied to people, food and gadgets alike.

en: dream guy or girl; exactly one's type

example.en: He's exactly my type.

note: 菜 = "type" (你是我的菜); 天菜 is the top grade. Originated in gay slang, now used by everyone, mostly by women about men.

en: to catch feelings (for a fling or casual date)

example.zh: 才約會兩次，我好像暈船了。
example.en: We've only been on two dates and I think I've caught feelings.

note: "Seasick": falling for someone who is not serious about you. Since about 2019; 暈爛 = hopelessly hooked. Dating-app vocabulary.

example.en: I'm a loner in my class.

note: Popular among students since about 2015. Mostly self-mocking: eating alone, nobody to team up with. 邊緣 alone works as an adjective: 我很邊緣.

en: guy used for favors (rides, errands) with no romance in return

example.zh: 他只是她的工具人，負責接送。
example.en: He's just her errand boy, in charge of driving her around.

note: A man exploited by his crush, or anyone valued only for being useful. PTT-born. Mainland 舔狗 stresses fawning; 工具人 stresses being used.

example.en: You're too much, lol.

note: A sideways laughing face. The signature Taiwanese texting laugh, softer than 哈哈 and used to soften almost any message. Mainlanders rarely use it.

example.en: My report is gone, so sad.

note: Two teary eyes. In Taiwan QQ means sad, not the Tencent app. It also means "chewy" for food (QQ的), so context decides.

example.zh: 他只回我呵呵，是不是生氣了？
example.en: He just replied "hehe". Is he mad?

note: In Taiwanese texting 呵呵 is almost never friendly; it signals "I'm done with this". For real laughter use 哈哈 or XD.

example.zh: 笑死，他居然穿拖鞋來面試。
example.en: LOL, he actually wore flip-flops to the interview.

note: The default reaction to anything funny, spoken and typed. Stronger: 笑爛, 笑到往生. Cutesy respelling: 笑鼠.

en: "elder memes": greeting images older relatives send on LINE

example.zh: 我媽每天早上都傳長輩圖。
example.en: My mom sends an elder greeting image every morning.

note: Flowers or sunsets with 早安 and life advice in bold type. A beloved national joke; young people now make ironic ones.

example.en: My phone fell in the toilet. It's done for.

note: From gamers' "good game" at the end of a match. Means failure or doom: 我GG了. GG is also a nickname for TSMC and a crude word, so context matters.

example.en: I want to order fried chicken too, +1.

note: Used in group chats to join an order or agree; spoken as 加一. In group buys, 喊+1 commits you to buying.

example.en: My internet is really laggy today.

note: Taiwan says lag for network delay where the mainland says 卡. Also of people: 你很lag欸 = you're slow to catch on.

example.en: He only replies that fast because he likes you.

note: Also 秒讀 (read instantly) and 秒殺 (sell out in seconds). In dating talk, reply speed counts as evidence.

example.zh: 你有看到她昨天的限動嗎？
example.en: Did you see her story from yesterday?

note: Short for 限時動態. 發限動 = post a story. An everyday word for anyone under 40.

en: social media admin (of a brand or page)

example.zh: 這個粉專的小編很幽默。
example.en: The admin of this page is really funny.

note: The person behind a brand's posts, addressed directly in comments (小編加薪). Some government agencies' 小編 are minor celebrities.

example.zh: 他們的粉專有公告營業時間。
example.en: Their Facebook page lists the opening hours.

note: Short for 粉絲專頁. Small shops often have a 粉專 instead of a website, so check it for hours and menus.

example.zh: 這間網美咖啡廳要排很久。
example.en: There's a long wait for this Instagram-famous café.

note: Short for 網路美女. 網美店, 網美牆, 網美照 describe anything built for photos. Can be mildly mocking: all looks, no substance.

example.en: Just ignore those haters.

note: 酸 "sour" = sarcastic. People who leave sneering comments. The mainland says 喷子 or 键盘侠.

example.en: This meme has been really popular lately.

note: Transliteration of "meme". 迷因圖 and 梗圖 are interchangeable. The mainland uses 梗 and 表情包.

example.en: That joke is really old by now.

note: From 哏 via Taiwanese variety shows; later spread to the mainland. 有梗 = witty, 老梗 = stale, 梗圖 = meme image, 鋪梗 = set up a joke.

example.zh: 我買了一組新的貓咪貼圖。
example.en: I bought a new set of cat stickers.

note: LINE stickers are a huge part of Taiwanese chatting; a sticker often replaces the reply. The mainland says 表情包.

en: LINE (the messaging app); to message on LINE

example.en: Message me on LINE and I'll reply later.

note: Sound-loan of LINE, Taiwan's default messenger. 加賴 = add on LINE. An informal spelling; people also just type LINE.

example.zh: 我把你加進我們的群組。
example.en: I'll add you to our group chat.

note: A LINE group. The mainland says 群 or 群聊. 退群組 = leave the group; the 家族群組 is where 長輩圖 flow.

example.zh: 我已經把前男友封鎖了。
example.en: I've already blocked my ex-boyfriend.

note: The term on LINE, IG and Facebook. The mainland says 拉黑. 解除封鎖 = unblock.

en: nonsense said with a straight face; BS

example.en: The boss was spouting nonsense in the meeting again.

note: A 2017 buzzword: empty or absurd statements delivered confidently. 講幹話 can be affectionate (witty nonsense) or scornful. Crude character, printable usage.

en: useless teammate who makes things worse

example.zh: 我老公是豬隊友，越幫越忙。
example.en: My husband is a useless teammate; his help makes things worse.

note: From gaming; used widely by wives about husbands. Opposite: 神隊友. Shared with the mainland.

example.zh: 我是I人，聚會完要休息兩天。
example.en: I'm an introvert; I need two days to recover after a party.

note: MBTI talk swept Taiwan from Korea around 2022–2023. I人 and E人 (extrovert) are now ordinary self-descriptions among under-35s.

en: excuse me; sorry; (also) thanks for the trouble

example.zh: 不好意思，請問廁所在哪裡？
example.en: Excuse me, where's the restroom?

note: Taiwan's universal social lubricant: it opens requests, apologizes for small things and even thanks people. 對不起 is kept for real fault. Use it far more than feels necessary.

example.en: Excuse me, coming through.

note: What you say on the MRT or in a crowd, usually softened as 借過一下 or prefixed with 不好意思. Mainland speakers often say 让一下.

en: "if you would, please"; sorry to trouble you

example.en: Could you bag it for me, please? Thanks.

note: Polite request opener or closer: 麻煩你了 = thanks in advance. With staff, 麻煩 + verb is the standard courteous order: 麻煩給我一杯水.

example.en: Thanks for your hard work today; head home early.

note: Said to colleagues at day's end, delivery riders, drivers, anyone who did something for you. A warm sign-off, more routine than on the mainland.

example.en: Please, don't be late again.

note: Two uses: sincere pleading (拜託你了) and an exasperated "give me a break" with a drawn-out 拜～託. Tone decides which.

en: it's okay, don't worry about it

example.zh: 沒關係啦，下次再約就好。
example.en: It's okay, we'll just meet up another time.

note: Taiwan says xì with a full tone. 啦 makes the reassurance warmer. The standard answer to 不好意思 and 對不起.

example.en: "Thank you, teacher." "You're welcome."

note: Correct but a little formal; in daily life Taiwanese more often answer thanks with 不會. Full tone on 氣 in Taiwan.

example.en: "Your Chinese is so good!" "Oh, it's nothing special."

note: The reflex reply to praise or sympathy; accepting a compliment outright can seem immodest. See also 沒有啦.

en: "no, not really" (deflecting praise; softening a denial)

example.en: "You've lost weight!" "Nah, not really."

note: Modest denial with a smile. Also softens corrections: 沒有啦，我是說明天. Constant in Taiwanese conversation.

example.en: I'm easy; you decide.

note: Easygoing when said lightly, but it can sound careless or sulky (隨便你 = suit yourself). 都可以 and 看你 are the safer polite versions.

example.en: Anywhere's fine; I'm not picky.

note: The polite non-answer Taiwanese give to almost every choice. Mainland speakers say 都行. Expect a few rounds of 都可以 before anyone decides.

example.en: Do you want to go? It's up to you.

note: Hands the decision back. Friendly with a light tone; with a flat tone it means "do what you want, I don't care".

example.en: "Want to see a movie together?" "Sure!"

note: Willing, upbeat acceptance of a suggestion. Compare 好喔 (compliant okay), 好啦 (fine, I give in), 可以啊 (works for me).

example.en: Saturday? Sure, I'm free.

note: Agreeable but a shade less eager than 好啊. Mainland speakers would mostly say 行啊; 行 is rare in Taiwan.

example.en: Seriously? He's getting married?

note: A reaction of surprise, not an accusation of lying. Shortened to 真假. One of the most frequent reactions in Taiwanese chat.

example.zh: 你很誇張欸，遲到一個小時。
example.en: You're unbelievable. An hour late!

note: The pattern 你很…欸 delivers mock or real reproach: 你很煩欸, 你很慢欸. Among friends it is teasing.

en: what do I do? what now?

example.zh: 我的手機不見了，怎麼辦？
example.en: My phone's gone. What do I do?

note: Shared with the mainland, but Taiwanese say it constantly as a mild "oh no", often expecting no answer. Cutesy doubling: 怎麼辦怎麼辦.

en: nothing can be done; can't help it

example.zh: 沒辦法，公司規定就是這樣。
example.en: Can't be helped; that's company policy.

note: Resigned acceptance. Also a soft refusal: 我明天沒辦法 = I can't make it tomorrow. Full third tone on 法.

example.en: Forget it, don't bother arguing with him.

note: Dropping a matter or consoling someone. Said sharply, 算了 means "fine, forget I asked".

example.en: Are you free this weekend?

note: The usual lead-in to an invitation. Answering 怎麼了？ ("what's up?") before committing is normal.

example.zh: 今天太累了，改天再去吧。
example.en: I'm too tired today; let's go another day.

note: Often a polite brush-off: 改天再約 or 改天請你吃飯 may never happen. A real plan names a date.

example.en: Something's come up today; let's reschedule.

note: Standard friendly parting or postponement. 約 = arrange to meet: 約吃飯, 約時間. Like 改天, it can be noncommittal.

example.zh: 今天我請客，不要跟我搶。
example.en: It's my treat today; don't fight me for the bill.

note: Short form: 我請. Expect a ritual tussle over the bill among older people; younger friends usually split.

en: each pays their own; to go Dutch

example.en: Let's just each pay for our own.

note: The Taiwan way to say "split the bill"; the mainland says AA. To the cashier say 分開結 or 分開算.

example.en: Hi, for here or to go?

note: The first question at any counter. The mainland says 堂食 or 在这吃. Just answer 內用 or 外帶.

example.en: One hot latte, to go.

note: The mainland says 打包 or 带走; in Taiwan 打包 means boxing up leftovers. Also a modifier: 外帶杯.

example.en: Excuse me, we'd like the bill.

note: For sit-down restaurants; many eateries have you pay at the counter (櫃檯結帳). 結帳 is equally common.

example.en: I have a carrier barcode; no need to print the receipt.

note: Taiwan's receipts are lottery tickets; a 載具 (the phone barcode, 手機條碼) stores them electronically. Cashiers ask 有載具嗎？ constantly.

en: company tax ID (for a business receipt)

example.en: Do you need a tax ID on the receipt?

note: Short for 統一編號. Asked at every register; unless you are expensing the purchase, answer 不用.

example.en: That's two hundred in total. Need a bag?

note: Plastic bags cost NT$1–2, so every cashier asks. Answer 不用 or 要一個. Also 需要購物袋嗎？

example.en: Table for two? This way, please.

note: Staff formula. Taiwan service speech puts 這邊 everywhere: 這邊幫您結帳, 這邊跟您確認一下.

example.en: Okay, just a moment please.

note: The standard friendly "hold on" from staff; 喔 softens it. More formal: 請稍等, 請稍候.

example.zh: 請問一下，捷運站怎麼走？
example.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the MRT station?

note: 一下 makes the question feel small and polite. Often preceded by 不好意思 for double softening.

example.en: No problem, I'll send it to you tomorrow.

note: Reassuring acceptance of a request. Shared with the mainland; in Taiwan often followed by 啦 or 喔.

example.en: Certainly, I'll take care of it right away.

note: The polite, professional okay for customers, bosses and emails. With friends it can feel distant; use 好喔 or 好啊.

example.zh: 了解，那我們改到星期五。
example.en: Got it, so we'll move it to Friday.

note: A common acknowledgment in work chat. Neutral-polite and warmer than a bare 好. Also written 瞭解.

example.en: Got it, thanks for the reminder.

note: Work-chat confirmation that you saw a message or instruction. Crisp; add 謝謝 to keep it friendly.

en: you can do it! hang in there!

example.en: Good luck at your interview tomorrow!

note: Shared with the mainland but used for everything in Taiwan, even as a goodbye to someone busy or stressed. 加油加油 is extra warm.

example.en: Take your time; we're in no hurry.

note: Kind reassurance. With 啦 it also calms someone who is flustered.

en: get home safe; take care on the way

example.en: It's late; get home safe.

note: The standard parting to anyone leaving. For scooter riders: 騎車小心.

example.en: The road's slippery in the rain; ride safe.

note: Scooters are the default transport, so this is an everyday goodbye. For drivers: 開車小心.

en: text me when you get home

example.zh: 時間不早了，到家跟我說。
example.en: It's getting late; text me when you get home.

note: A routine caring sign-off among friends and couples after a night out. The expected reply is just 到了.

example.en: Good morning, what would you like to drink today?

note: Taiwan says 早安, 午安, 晚安; mainland 早上好 sounds foreign here. Among friends just 早.

example.en: I'm off to bed, good night.

note: The bedtime sign-off in chats; also the formal evening greeting on TV and at events (各位觀眾晚安).

example.en: I'm heading home then, bye-bye.

note: The default goodbye; 再見 sounds formal or final. Taiwan writes 掰掰 (first tone) to keep it apart from 拜拜 "to worship".

example.en: I'm off to a meeting first; see you later.

note: Taiwan uses 晚點 for "later on": 晚點再說, 晚點回你. No 兒化: never 一會兒見.

en: wait a moment; in a bit, later

example.en: I'll call you back in a bit.

note: Besides "wait", it is the Taiwan way to say "later" (等一下去吃飯). Mainland 一会儿 and 待会儿 with 兒化 are not used.

example.en: I'm going to the convenience store in a bit.

note: As a time word it equals 等一下: 等等見 = see you in a bit. A favorite in texting.

example.en: Coming right up, one moment please.

note: Shared with the mainland. Staff say 馬上來 or 馬上好; whether it is truly immediate is another matter.

example.en: I called you just now.

note: Taiwan uses 剛剛 where the mainland prefers 刚才. Note the 有 + verb past in the example, also very Taiwanese.

example.en: Long time no see. How've you been?

note: Taiwan drops the 麼: 怎樣 rather than 怎么样. A casual catch-up opener; answer 還不錯, 老樣子 or 很忙.

example.en: The coffee here is pretty good.

note: Mild praise that often simply means "good". 不錯喔 with a rising tone = "hey, nice!".

example.en: Hi auntie, have you eaten?

note: The Mandarin version of Taiwanese 呷飽未. A greeting to neighbors and elders, not an invitation. Answer 吃飽了, whatever the truth.

example.en: Hello, is anybody here?

note: The everyday informal greeting, also used to hail staff or start a call. A sarcastic 哈囉？ = "hello, are you even listening?".

example.en: Thanks! Next time it's on me.

note: Breezy thanks between friends. More formal: 謝謝你; warmer: 感謝, 感恩.

example.en: Sorry, I'll be ten minutes late.

note: Sits between 不好意思 (light) and 對不起 (serious). Common in texts and work messages; often doubled: 抱歉抱歉.

example.en: No thanks, I'll do it myself.

note: The polite refusal for bags, receipts, flyers and offers of help. Soften with 謝謝. 不用啦 is the friendly version.

example.en: Oh don't, I'd be embarrassed.

note: Protesting or coyly refusing. Tone ranges from playful to pleading. A flat 不要 is much blunter.

example.en: All right, enough, stop arguing.

note: Tells someone to stop nagging, joking or fighting. Milder than 夠了. 我好了 separately means "I'm done / ready".

example.en: Come off it, you're obviously happy.

note: Brushes off flattery, excuses or false modesty. Friendly banter; not for superiors.

example.en: You say you're busy? Yeah, right.

note: Literally "it had better be": sarcastic disbelief. Usually 最好是啦, or 最好是 + the doubtful claim. Peers only.

example.en: Him, on time? Not a chance.

note: Tacked onto a statement to deny it. Playful; common from kids and between friends.

example.en: "This really is good." "Right?!"

note: Besides the ordinary question, a triumphant 是不是！ claims victory after the other person concedes your point.

en: "really? did I? I don't think so"

example.en: "You've lost weight again." "Have I?"

note: A mild challenge to someone's observation. It rests on Taiwan's 有 + verb pattern (你有說嗎？).

example.en: "Did you bring an umbrella?" "Yeah, I did."

note: Taiwan Mandarin uses 有 as a past or experience marker (我有去, 你有看到嗎), from Taiwanese ū. So 有啊 answers "did you...?"; a mainlander would say 带了.

example.zh: 我想說你在忙，就沒打給你。
example.en: I figured you were busy, so I didn't call.

note: Calqued on Taiwanese siūnn-kóng. Reports your reasoning, often to explain or excuse an action. One of the surest markers of Taiwan Mandarin.

example.zh: 我跟你說，他們兩個在一起了。
example.en: Guess what, those two are together now.

note: Announces gossip or an opinion. 我跟你講 is the more Taiwanese-flavored variant. 我跟你說喔 = "listen, okay?".

en: "by the way; come to think of it"

example.en: By the way, what time do you get off tomorrow?

note: A sentence opener that shifts topic or adds an afterthought. Very Taiwanese; the mainland uses 话说.

example.en: "You cooked this yourself?" "Well, who else?"

note: A cheeky comeback implying the answer is obvious. 啊不然咧 is the fuller Taiwanese-flavored form. Rude to elders.

example.en: You keep staring at me. What's the deal?

note: Often 現在是怎樣. Puzzled or confrontational depending on tone; calqued on Taiwanese 是按怎.

en: what are you doing?; why?; what for?

example.en: What are you up to? Want to come out?

note: 你在幹嘛 is the standard "what's up" text. Alone, 幹嘛？ = "what do you want?". 幹嘛這樣 = "why are you being like this?".

example.zh: 他只是客氣，你想太多了。
example.en: He's just being polite; you're reading too much into it.

note: Reassures a worrier or deflates a hopeful. A blunt 你想太多 = "in your dreams".

example.en: You got in? That's wonderful!

note: Taiwan praise leans on 好 + adjective + 喔 (好棒, 好厲害, 好可愛), which sounds gentle, even girlish, to mainland ears. Men use it too.

example.zh: 你會說五種語言？好厲害！
example.en: You speak five languages? Impressive!

note: The all-purpose compliment; as a learner you will hear 你中文好厲害 daily. Reply 沒有啦 or 還好啦. Full tone on 害.

example.zh: 你下個月要去日本？好好喔。
example.en: You're going to Japan next month? Lucky you.

note: Expresses friendly envy. A very Taiwanese construction; the mainland says 真好 or 好羡慕.

example.en: Oh my god, how could this happen!

note: Shock, dismay or delight. Variants: 我的天啊, 天哪. Taiwan favors 天啊.

example.en: Happy New Year, everyone. Cheers!

note: In Taiwan 乾杯 literally obliges you to empty the glass; if you cannot, say 隨意 (sip as you like) or 半杯.

example.en: All the dishes are here. Let's dig in!

note: Announces the start of a meal, like Japanese itadakimasu. 我要開動了 is cute and common in posts.

example.zh: 您的餐點到齊了，請慢用。
example.en: That's all your dishes. Enjoy your meal.

note: The waiter's formula when serving. No reply needed beyond 謝謝.

example.en: Welcome! How many in your party?

note: Called out at the door of every shop and convenience store. You need not respond. The exit line is 謝謝光臨.

example.en: How many will be dining?

note: The first question at any restaurant. Answer with a number + 位 or 個: 兩位, 三個.

example.en: I have a reservation under Chen, for two.

note: Taiwan says 訂位; the mainland says 订座 or 预订. Staff ask 有訂位嗎？ Popular places need booking weeks ahead.

example.en: Can I pay by card?

note: Many small eateries are cash only (只收現金), so ask. Mobile payment is 行動支付, or people just name the app: LINE Pay.

example.en: I didn't bring a card; is cash okay?

note: Short for 付現金. The cashier's question: 刷卡還是付現？ Cash remains king at night markets and small shops.

example.en: Remember to tap your card when you board.

note: Named after the beep. The colloquial verb for tapping an EasyCard on buses, at MRT gates and in shops. Also written 逼卡.

example.en: Hi, are you a member?

note: A standard cashier question at chains. Answer 沒有, or give your phone number (報電話) to collect points.

example.en: Would you like this lunchbox heated?

note: A convenience-store ritual for boxed meals and buns. Answer 要 or 不用. Also 需要微波嗎？

en: "boss": how you address any shopkeeper or stall owner

example.en: Boss, one fried chicken cutlet, not spicy.

note: The normal way to hail a vendor of either sex; a woman can also be 老闆娘 or 闆娘. Mainland 服务员 is not used in Taiwan.

en: "handsome": a vendor's address for any male customer

example.en: Hey handsome, what are you after today?

note: Market and shop talk: every man is 帥哥 and every woman 美女, regardless of looks. Take it as friendliness, not flirting.

example.en: Miss, you dropped something.

note: Perfectly polite in Taiwan, unlike on the mainland where it can suggest a sex worker. Used for strangers and after surnames: 陳小姐.

example.en: Hey, you need to queue here.

note: Shop staff, guards and teachers use it for anyone who looks like a student, up to about 25.

en: "big brother": polite address for a slightly older man

example.zh: 大哥，請問這附近有郵局嗎？
example.en: Excuse me, sir, is there a post office near here?

note: Safe, friendly address for drivers, repairmen and strangers; women are 大姊. Taiwan does not call drivers 師傅.

example.zh: 我昨天去逛街，然後買了鞋子。
example.en: I went shopping yesterday and, like, bought shoes.

note: The signature Taiwanese filler: young speakers start half their sentences with it, often slurred to nánhòu. It need not mean sequence.

example.en: "He's too much." "I know, right."

note: 就是說啊 = strong agreement. Mid-sentence, 就是說 or 就是 is a filler while searching for words.

example.en: Um, I'd like to ask something.

note: Said nèi ge (or nà ge) while thinking, or to open a delicate request. Also a euphemism: 那個來了 = my period came.

example.en: Thanks, I'm just looking.

note: The polite way to fend off a shop assistant. They will answer 好的，有需要再跟我說.

example.zh: 你今天也累了，早點休息。
example.en: You've had a tiring day too; get some rest.

note: A friendly way to close a late chat. Taiwan says xiū xí with a full second tone.

example.en: You guys pick the time; I'm fine with anything.

note: OK is fully part of Taiwan Mandarin: OK啊, OK的, 不OK. The same accommodating spirit as 都可以.

example.zh: 我要一杯珍珠奶茶，半糖少冰。
example.en: One bubble tea, half sugar, less ice.

note: Invented in Taiwan in the 1980s and usually shortened to 珍奶. Big pearls are 波霸. An order always includes a sugar level and an ice level.

example.en: Want to order shaken drinks this afternoon?

note: The collective term for tea-shop drinks; the shops are 手搖店 or 飲料店. Offices order in groups almost daily (訂飲料).

example.en: Green tea, half sugar, no ice, thanks.

note: The sugar scale runs 全糖 (正常), 少糖, 半糖, 微糖, 無糖. State it right after the drink name.

example.en: Light sugar is sweet enough for me.

note: Taiwan reads 微 as wéi (second tone), not mainland wēi. The most popular choice among health-minded drinkers.

example.en: I'd like an unsweetened oolong tea.

note: For pure teas. With fruit drinks, staff may warn you 無糖會比較酸.

example.en: Milk tea, no ice, light sugar.

note: The ice scale: 正常冰, 少冰, 微冰, 去冰, then 常溫, 溫, 熱. A 去冰 drink is still cold; 完全去冰 means none at all.

example.en: Black tea latte, less ice, half sugar.

note: The safe default. Sugar and ice can come in either order: 半糖少冰 or 少冰半糖.

example.zh: 我要一杯大杯的冬瓜檸檬。
example.en: A large winter melon lemonade, please.

note: Most tea shops have 中杯 and 大杯; a 大杯 is about 700 ml. Convenience-store coffee comes in 中, 大, 特大.

example.zh: 老闆，一碗滷肉飯加滷蛋。
example.en: Boss, one braised pork rice with a braised egg.

note: The national comfort food. In the south the same dish is 肉燥飯, and 滷肉飯 there may mean a slab of pork belly (the north's 控肉飯).

example.zh: 下班買一塊雞排當晚餐。
example.en: I buy a chicken cutlet for dinner after work.

note: A face-sized night-market staple. The vendor asks 要切嗎？要辣嗎？ The classic indulgence is 雞排配珍奶.

en: Taiwanese popcorn chicken (and mixed fried snacks)

example.zh: 宵夜我們買鹹酥雞好不好？
example.en: How about we get popcorn chicken for a late-night snack?

note: You pick items into a basket and they are fried with basil and garlic. Also written 鹽酥雞. The definitive guilty late-night snack.

example.zh: 我早餐都點蛋餅配豆漿。
example.en: For breakfast I always order an egg crepe with soy milk.

note: The breakfast-shop classic: a thin wrapper fried with egg, rolled and sliced, with soy paste. Variants: 起司蛋餅, 玉米蛋餅.

example.zh: 早上買一個飯糰當早餐。
example.en: I buy a rice ball in the morning for breakfast.

note: The Taiwanese breakfast kind is a fist of sticky rice around fried dough, pork floss and pickles. Convenience stores sell the Japanese triangular kind (御飯糰).

example.en: Let's order two baskets of soup dumplings.

note: Made world-famous by Din Tai Fung (鼎泰豐). Breakfast shops sell a thicker-skinned, soupless version under the same name.

example.en: The stinky tofu at the night market smells great.

note: Deep-fried with pickled cabbage, or stewed and spicy (麻辣臭豆腐). Taiwanese are delighted when a foreigner likes it. Full tone on 腐.

example.zh: 來夜市一定要點蚵仔煎。
example.en: You have to order an oyster omelet at the night market.

note: Always said in Taiwanese: ô-á-tsian. Oysters, egg and greens in a chewy starch batter with a sweet-savory sauce.

example.en: I'd like a bowl of tofu pudding with peanuts.

note: Served sweet in Taiwan, in syrup with peanuts, tapioca or red beans, cold or warm. Savory northern-style 豆腐腦 is not a thing here.

example.zh: 下班我們去熱炒店喝啤酒。
example.en: After work let's go to a stir-fry place and drink beer.

note: Noisy, cheap restaurants (熱炒店, 快炒店, often "百元熱炒") for group dinners with Taiwan Beer. The Taiwanese answer to a pub night.

example.zh: 我家樓下有一間早餐店。
example.en: There's a breakfast shop downstairs from my place.

note: Either Western-style (漢堡, 蛋餅, 奶茶) or a soy-milk shop (豆漿店). The owner famously calls everyone 帥哥 and 美女.

example.en: Let's go wander the night market tonight.

note: You 逛 a night market. Every city has several; locals prefer neighborhood ones over the famous tourist ones.

example.en: Tainan's street food is the most famous.

note: Small-portion local dishes that define Taiwanese food culture. 小吃店 = a humble eatery; 台灣小吃 is a source of pride.

example.en: The black tea here is the old-fashioned kind.

note: From Taiwanese kóo-tsá-bī. Nostalgic praise for food made the traditional way: 古早味蛋糕, 古早味紅茶. Also for retro shops and toys.

example.en: The pearls here are really chewy.

note: From Taiwanese khiū. The key Taiwanese texture word, for pearls, noodles, fish balls and mochi. Intensified as QQ or Q彈. Written with the Latin letter.

example.en: This mapo tofu goes great with rice.

note: Praise for salty, saucy dishes. Shared with the mainland. Related: 下酒菜 (drinking snacks).

example.zh: 這家火鍋吃到飽只要五百。
example.en: All-you-can-eat hot pot here is only five hundred.

note: Taiwan's word for a buffet (the mainland says 自助餐, which in Taiwan is a pay-by-dish cafeteria). Also unlimited mobile data: 網路吃到飽.

example.en: I'll have a bowl of braised beef noodle soup.

note: A national dish, born in military dependents' villages. Choose 紅燒 (soy-braised) or 清燉 (clear broth); add 酸菜 at the table.

en: braised snacks picked from a display

example.en: How about braised snacks for a late-night bite?

note: You pick tofu, noodles, vegetables and meats into a basket; they are reheated in soy broth (加熱滷味) or served cold.

example.zh: 便利商店的茶葉蛋很香。
example.en: The tea eggs at convenience stores smell so good.

note: Simmering in every convenience store; the smell is part of Taiwan. Also a meme since a 2011 mainland TV pundit claimed Taiwanese could not afford them.

example.zh: 中午去自助餐夾菜比較便宜。
example.en: Picking dishes at the cafeteria is cheaper for lunch.

note: A false friend: in Taiwan it is a point-and-pick cafeteria priced by item or weight, not an all-you-can-eat buffet (that is 吃到飽).

example.zh: 天氣一冷，麻辣鍋就要排隊。
example.en: As soon as it gets cold, there's a line for spicy hot pot.

note: Taiwan's take features duck blood and tofu (鴨血豆腐) with free refills. Usually ordered as 鴛鴦鍋 (half spicy, half mild).

example.zh: 肚子餓了，要不要買宵夜？
example.en: I'm hungry. Want to get a late-night snack?

note: Taiwan says 宵夜; the mainland says 夜宵. A social institution: 鹹酥雞, 滷味, soy-milk shops, 清粥小菜.

example.zh: 這間咖啡廳低消一杯飲料。
example.en: This café has a one-drink minimum.

note: Short for 最低消費. Posted at most cafés and bars, usually per person, and often paired with a time limit (用餐限時九十分鐘).

example.en: I'll have the house special lunchbox.

note: On menus 招牌 marks the dish a place is known for. When unsure, order the 招牌.

example.zh: 麻煩一份小辣，不要香菜。
example.en: One mild, no cilantro, please.

note: The spice scale: 不辣, 微辣, 小辣, 中辣, 大辣. Taiwanese heat levels run milder than Sichuan or Hunan ones.

example.en: Coffee is buy-one-get-one today.

note: Convenience-store coffee and tea-shop promotions; people 揪 a friend to share. Related: 第二杯半價.

example.zh: 我想去在地人推薦的店。
example.en: I want to go where the locals recommend.

note: From Taiwanese tsāi-tē. 在地人 = locals; 在地美食, 在地食材. Warmer than 本地 or 當地; it signals real local roots.

example.en: The Thai food here is really authentic.

note: Taiwan says 道地; the mainland flips it to 地道. A classic pair to swap when you switch sides of the strait.

example.en: At a stir-fry joint you obviously drink Taiwan Beer.

note: Short for 台灣啤酒. The premium label is 金牌; 18天 is the fresh draft type with an 18-day shelf life.

en: to hit on girls, to pick up girls

example.zh: 他很會把妹，女友一直換。
example.en: He's good at picking up girls; he keeps changing girlfriends.

note: Taiwan's standard casual term; 妹 is usually said mēi here. Slightly crude but common. When the woman does the chasing it is 倒追.

example.en: He pursued her for half a year before it worked.

note: The normal verb for courting: 追女生, 很多人追. 倒追 = the woman pursues the man. 追到了 = won her over.

example.en: I've decided to tell her how I feel tomorrow.

note: Taiwan says 告白 (from Japanese kokuhaku); the mainland says 表白. A relationship usually starts officially with a 告白, so 告白失敗 is a big deal.

en: flirty ambiguity; the "something's going on" stage

example.zh: 他們還在曖昧，沒有在一起。
example.en: They're still in the flirting stage, not together yet.

note: Mutual interest before any commitment: 搞曖昧, 曖昧對象. A recognized stage of Taiwanese dating, immortalized in pop songs.

en: to be together (as a couple); to start dating

example.en: We've been together for three years.

note: Marks official couple status: 你們在一起了嗎？ Friends chant 在一起！在一起！ at a public confession.

en: to date, to be in a relationship

example.en: They've been dating for two years.

note: The standard, slightly formal word: 交往中, 穩定交往 (going steady), 以結婚為前提交往. The mainland says 谈恋爱.

example.en: They broke up last month.

note: Shared with the mainland. 提分手 = initiate it; 被分手 = get dumped; 和平分手 = an amicable split.

en: to cheat on a partner, to two-time

example.zh: 她發現男友劈腿，氣到大哭。
example.en: She found out her boyfriend was cheating and cried with rage.

note: "Doing the splits" between two people. The Taiwan word for cheating while dating; 外遇 and 出軌 are for marriages. Taiwan says pī.

example.zh: 原來她是介入別人感情的小三。
example.en: Turns out she was the other woman who came between them.

note: From 第三者. Shared with the mainland. The male version is 小王. A staple of news and TV dramas.

example.zh: 你的另一半是做什麼的？
example.en: What does your partner do?

note: Neutral as to gender and marital status, so it is the tactful way to ask about someone's partner. Mainland 对象 is not used in Taiwan.

example.en: Her boyfriend is an engineer.

note: Clipped form of 男朋友, common in speech and headlines. 前男友 = ex-boyfriend. A male friend who is not a boyfriend is a 男生朋友.

example.en: He brought his girlfriend home to meet his parents.

note: Clipped form of 女朋友. A 女生朋友 is merely a friend who is a woman. 前女友 = ex-girlfriend.

example.en: I don't want to stay in touch with my ex.

note: Gender-neutral; 前男友 and 前女友 are specific, 現任 = current partner. Ex stories fill Dcard's relationship board (感情版).

example.zh: 我跟別的女生講話他就吃醋。
example.en: He gets jealous whenever I talk to another girl.

note: Shared with the mainland. A jealous type is a 醋桶 or 醋罈子. Mild, often cute.

en: to have a secret crush on

example.zh: 我暗戀隔壁班的同學很久了。
example.en: I've had a secret crush on someone in the next class for ages.

note: Liking someone without telling them; the person is your 暗戀對象. The next step is 告白.

en: to chat someone up, to approach a stranger

example.en: Someone chatted me up at a café.

note: Approaching strangers is less common in Taiwan than apps or friends' introductions, so 被搭訕 is a story worth telling.

en: "nice-guy card": rejection with "you're a good person"

example.zh: 我告白失敗，又收到好人卡。
example.en: My confession failed; I got the nice-guy card again.

note: From the stock rejection 你是個好人. A PTT coinage that spread across the Chinese-speaking world. 收卡 = get rejected.

example.en: I don't want to be someone's backup.

note: The person kept around in case the first choice falls through. Shared with the mainland.

example.en: Congrats on finally getting out of singlehood!

note: A mainland-origin term, fully adopted. The PTT-flavored equivalent is 脫魯. Singles wish each other 早日脫單.

example.zh: 我要跟姊妹淘去喝下午茶。
example.en: I'm going for afternoon tea with my girlfriends.

note: The native Taiwan term; mainland-origin 閨蜜 is now equally common among the young. Taiwan writes 姊 and says jiě.

example.zh: 她是我從高中到現在的閨蜜。
example.en: She's been my bestie since high school.

note: Arrived from the mainland in the 2010s and stuck. More intimate than 姊妹淘. 男閨蜜 = a platonic male bestie.

example.en: Don't worry, your bros have your back.

note: Male bonding term. 好兄弟 = great buddy, but also a euphemism for ghosts. Mainland 哥們兒 is not used. Full tone on 弟.

en: close buddy; to get along great

example.zh: 我們兩個從小就很麻吉。
example.en: The two of us have been tight since we were kids.

note: From English "match", probably via Japanese. Noun or adjective: 好麻吉, 很麻吉. Informal and friendly.

example.en: He's my best buddy from junior high.

note: A friend of unconditional loyalty, usually from school days. Either gender.

example.zh: 那間飲料店的店員是正妹。
example.en: The girl working at that drink shop is a babe.

note: 正 = hot; 妹 is usually said mēi here. Ubiquitous in media (正妹主播). Fine among friends; to her face say 妳很漂亮.

en: to feel a spark, to click romantically

example.en: I feel absolutely no spark with him.

note: "The current arrives". Mostly negated: 不來電. 被電到 = zapped by someone's charm; 放電 = give flirty looks.

example.zh: 她又遇到渣男，被騙感情。
example.en: She ran into another scumbag who toyed with her feelings.

note: Mainland-origin, universal on Dcard and Threads. 渣 works as an adjective: 他很渣. Female: 渣女.

example.zh: 她男友是媽寶，什麼都問媽媽。
example.en: Her boyfriend is a mama's boy who asks his mom about everything.

note: A top dating red flag on Taiwanese forums. From 媽媽的寶貝. Noun or adjective: 他很媽寶.

example.zh: 我媽又在情勒我回家住。
example.en: My mom is guilt-tripping me into moving back home again.

note: Short for 情緒勒索, from a 2017 bestseller. Used as a verb for partners, parents and bosses alike. The mainland talks of PUA or 道德绑架.

example.en: We did long-distance for two years.

note: Short for 遠距離戀愛; shorter still, 遠距. The mainland says 异地恋.

example.en: Ohh, you drank my drink!

note: Another spelling of 齁/吼. A drawn-out 厚～ is the classic "caught you!" tease used by kids and friends. Informal writing only.

example.en: I dunno either.

note: Playful respelling of 呢/耶 (also 餒, 內). Sounds cute and a bit airheaded; common in texting and among young women. Avoid it at work.

example.en: Careful, it's hot, sip it slowly.

note: Sweeter than 喔. Service staff and women use it to sound warm (歡迎再來唷); men use it less. Sentence-initial 唷 is a breezy "yo / oh my".

example.en: "Is it due tomorrow?" "Yep, tomorrow."

note: From Taiwanese hennh "yes". 嘿, 嘿啊, 嘿對 are relaxed ways to agree, heard more in central and southern Taiwan and from men. Earthier than 對.

example.en: Yeah, I think so too.

note: Taiwanese hennh-ah used inside Mandarin. Warmer and more local than 對啊; the cutesy variant is 嘿咩. Fine with friends and family, too folksy for formal talk.

example.en: I told you so, you never listen.

note: A cuter, whinier 嘛, from Taiwanese --mah. 對咩, 就是咩 = "exactly, duh". Sounds young and feminine; grown men mostly use it jokingly.

example.en: Good grief, why is it so expensive!

note: From Taiwanese ai-iō-uê. Exaggerated dismay or pain; it sounds like an auntie or grandma, so young people use it for comic effect.

example.en: Ugh, you're so slow!

note: Whining protest, often flirty or childish (撒嬌). Also 吼唷, 厚唷. More feeling than plain 齁 but not real anger. Mostly women and kids, or men being playful.

example.en: So how come you didn't come?

note: From Taiwanese ah. Opens questions and topic shifts: 啊你咧？ 啊不然咧？ Very local and folksy, typical of southern or older speakers; standard Mandarin has no such opener.

example.en: Well, I'm just tired, I don't want to go out.

note: From Taiwanese ah tō. Introduces an obvious or slightly defensive explanation. Casual and very Taiwanese; 啊不就 turns it sarcastic ("well isn't that just...").

example.en: No problem at all, leave it to me.

note: Adds a carefree, confident ring. It is also the stereotyped tag of indigenous-accented Mandarin, so do not use it to imitate people; that can offend.

example.en: Wait, hold on, why didn't you say so first?

note: Opens a protest or reality check; nothing is literally being negated. Very current among under-35s. Can sound confrontational toward superiors.

example.en: Whoa, this bowl is huge!

note: From a crude Taiwanese phrase but fully bleached: now a harmless "wow" that spread to the mainland in the 1990s. Slightly retro; 哇靠 is the cruder alternative.

example.en: Tsk, it's raining again.

note: A written-out tongue click. 嘖嘖 can be admiring or disapproving. Clicking at a person is rude, just as in English.

example.en: Pfft, who'd believe you.

note: A dismissive scoff; the Taiwan counterpart of mainland 切. Playful among friends, disrespectful toward elders.

example.en: This plot is way too ridiculous.

note: 很瞎 peaked around 2005–2015 and everyone still understands it, but under-25s now say 扯 or 傻眼 more. Used for situations, excuses, plots.

example.en: That customer was a total jerk.

note: Softened spelling of 機掰, from Taiwanese tsi-bai (female genitals). 雞歪 is rude but usable among friends; the original form is a fighting-words insult.

example.en: You're such a goof, why are you like this.

note: From Taiwanese sam-pat. Between female friends it is affectionate teasing; from a stranger or a man it is an insult. Slightly older-generation flavor.

example.zh: 老闆很阿莎力，直接打八折。
example.en: The boss was great about it, 20% off straight away.

note: From Japanese assari via Taiwanese a-sá-lih. A compliment for someone who decides fast and does not haggle. More common from people over 30.

en: to wheedle or pressure someone into a favor or discount

example.en: He's pushing me to cover his shift again.

note: From Taiwanese áu (拗). Pushing people for extras: 凹老闆送一份, 被客戶凹. The victim feels taken advantage of. Often written ㄠ.

example.zh: 我這個魯蛇只買得起泡麵。
example.en: A loser like me can only afford instant noodles.

note: Transliteration of "loser", from PTT around 2013. Mostly self-deprecating about pay, looks or being single. Opposite: 溫拿. Feels a bit 2010s now.

en: uptight; stubbornly holding back; keeping up a front

example.en: He's so stubborn about it, he won't even admit he's tired.

note: From Taiwanese; written in zhuyin for lack of an agreed character. Too proud or tense to relax or admit something. 不要ㄍㄧㄥ了 = stop holding out.

example.en: No need to pose so hard for a photo.

note: Same word as on the mainland, but a staple Taiwanese criticism of overdone cutesy behavior. Politer than 假掰.

example.en: This repairman is a bit hopeless.

note: From Taiwanese lióng-kong; often 很兩光. Folksy, used most by middle-aged speakers.

en: to slip up embarrassingly; to fall short of one's image

example.zh: 簡報到一半當機，超落漆。
example.en: The laptop froze mid-presentation. So embarrassing.

note: From Taiwanese lak-tshat "paint peeling off", and usually pronounced that way even mid-Mandarin. For performances and gadgets that fail at the key moment.

en: to be out of one's mind

example.en: Have you lost your mind?

note: Half-Mandarin rendering of Taiwanese thâu-khak pháinn-khì. Teasing between friends; the all-Mandarin version is 腦袋壞掉.

en: stubbornly skeptical; ignoring warnings or taboos

example.zh: 叫你帶傘你不帶，很鐵齒喔。
example.en: I told you to bring an umbrella and you wouldn't. So stubborn.

note: From Taiwanese thih-khí "iron teeth". Typically about ignoring superstitions, health advice or elders' warnings, then paying for it.

example.en: I called him by the wrong name. So embarrassing.

note: 糗了 = "I'm in trouble"; 出糗 = embarrass oneself; 糗他 = tease him. A Taiwan staple where the mainland uses 尴尬 or 丢人.

example.zh: 連這個都不會，你很遜欸。
example.en: You can't even do this? Lame.

note: 1990s–2000s school slang that never fully died; today it sounds a little dated or cute. Under-25s say 很爛, 很弱 or 很雷.

en: capable, reliable; to cover for, to back up

example.zh: 他電腦很罩，問他就對了。
example.en: He's great with computers, just ask him.

note: 很罩 = really good at something. 罩我一下 = help me out, cover for me. 罩得住 = can handle it. School and army flavor.

example.en: This shop has been really hot lately.

note: From Taiwanese hang "to heat". A 2000s buzzword now used mostly by news media and people over 35; younger people say 很紅 or 很火.

example.en: He loves telling dumb jokes.

note: From Taiwanese pe̍h-lān (crude origin). Annoyingly stupid behavior, or so-dumb-it's-funny humor. Also written 北爛.

example.en: He says he makes 100K a month. Total BS.

note: From Taiwanese hau-siâu; 洨 is literally semen, so it is cruder than 唬爛. Male-friend register only.

example.zh: 我對他這種態度很堵爛。
example.en: That attitude of his really pisses me off.

note: From Taiwanese tóo-lān (crude). Stronger than 不爽. Also written 賭爛. Not for polite company.

example.zh: 不要鳥他，他只是想吵架。
example.en: Ignore him, he just wants a fight.

note: 不鳥 or 懶得鳥 = ignore someone. 很鳥 = crappy; 鳥事 = annoying nonsense. Mildly crude (a softened 屌).

example.zh: 他們家的小狗無敵可愛。
example.en: Their puppy is insanely cute.

note: Goes before adjectives: 無敵可愛, 無敵累. Playful exaggeration, common in food reviews and among students.

example.zh: 你們真的很鬧，笑死我了。
example.en: You guys are ridiculous, I'm dying.

note: Goofy, absurd behavior, said fondly or in mock annoyance. 不要鬧了 = stop messing around, you're kidding.

example.en: Copying like that is really low.

note: English "low" dropped into Mandarin for cheap behavior or taste. Used on both sides of the strait.

example.en: He looks so manly when he drives.

note: A Taiwan-origin code-switch. A compliment for looks or decisive acts, said by women about men, or jokingly.

example.en: He gets totally goofy after drinking.

note: From Taiwanese; written in zhuyin. Originally "high on drugs", now mostly goofy or out of it. 你是ㄎㄧㄤ掉喔？ = have you lost it?

example.en: That accountant got caught skimming money.

note: The verb A "to pocket, to skim" (origin disputed, probably Taiwanese) is written with the Latin letter. Also A走, A東西. Common in news about officials.

en: hopeless klutz; someone who keeps blundering

example.en: The new coworker is a bit of a klutz.

note: From army slang for the recruit who botches everything. Fond exasperation rather than a harsh insult.

example.zh: 她很脫線，常常忘東忘西。
example.en: She's scatterbrained, always forgetting things.

note: "Off the rails": forgetful and prone to silly mistakes, often endearing. Mostly said about women or about oneself.

example.zh: 這門課很硬，很多人被當。
example.en: This course is brutal, lots of people fail.

note: 很硬 for courses, schedules, bosses. 硬要 = insist against all sense; 硬上 = push through anyway.

example.zh: 這堂課很涼，都不用點名。
example.en: This class is a breeze, no attendance taken.

note: 涼課 = easy-A class, 涼缺 = cushy post (army origin). In newer net slang 涼了 also means "it's dead, it flopped", as on the mainland.

example.zh: 這份工作很操，天天加班。
example.en: This job is grueling, overtime every day.

note: From military drills (操練). 被操 = get worked to the bone. In Taiwan 操 (cāo) is not the swear word that mainland cào is.

example.en: Hope you pass all your finals!

note: Sound-loan of "all pass". A finals-season blessing; students buy 歐趴糖 and lucky snacks.

example.en: He's an oddball, but a nice guy.

note: 咖 comes from Taiwanese kha (see 大咖). Ranges from affectionate to dismissive. Mainland 奇葩 is harsher.

example.zh: 這頓飯花了我三張小朋友。
example.en: This meal cost me three thousand-NT bills.

note: The NT$1,000 note shows four schoolchildren, hence the nickname. Jokey; mostly in speech and on PTT.

en: young office workers on modest pay

example.zh: 這間餐廳很適合小資族。
example.en: This restaurant is great for people on a modest salary.

note: In Taiwan 小資 means "small budget" (小資女, 小資旅行), unlike mainland 小资 = bourgeois-chic. Marketing loves the word.

example.zh: 一碗才三十塊，太佛心了。
example.en: Only thirty NT a bowl, that's so generous.

note: "Buddha-hearted": 佛心價, 佛心老闆, 佛心來著 (a PTT phrase). Praise for generosity that expects nothing back.

example.en: Two hundred a cup? You think I'm a sucker?

note: From Taiwanese phàn-á (fool), respelled 盤子. 好盤 = what a rip-off. Popular online since about 2015.

example.zh: 一顆茶葉蛋二十塊，搶錢喔。
example.en: Twenty NT for one tea egg? That's robbery.

note: An indignant complaint about prices, usually with 根本 or a final 喔. It targets the price, so it is safe to say among friends.

example.en: That move of yours is badass.

note: Crude (literally "dick") but common praise among young men. 屌打 = utterly outclass. 很屌 can also mean arrogant. Avoid around elders.

example.zh: 他一個人騎車環島，太狂了。
example.en: He rode around the whole island alone. Insane.

note: A buzzword since about 2016 (94狂 = 就是狂). 很狂, 太狂了 for bold or over-the-top feats and products.

example.zh: 大家都不講話，場面很乾。
example.en: Nobody was talking; it was really awkward.

note: When conversation dies: 很乾, 乾掉. Hosts work to keep the mood from 乾掉. Under-25s also borrow mainland 尬.

example.en: You're such a dawdler, hurry up.

note: Being slow to get ready or get going. Related: 摸魚 (slack off), 東摸西摸 (fiddle around).

example.en: Let's do all-night karaoke after exams.

note: KTV chains sell cheap midnight-to-dawn packages; a student rite of passage. Related: 夜衝, 夜遊.

example.zh: 我們昨天夜衝陽明山看夜景。
example.en: Last night we rode up Yangmingshan on a whim for the night view.

note: University scooter culture: ride off at midnight to a viewpoint, a beach or a 24-hour soy milk shop.

example.zh: 我們在辦公室聊天打屁。
example.en: We were shooting the breeze in the office.

note: Usually 聊天打屁 or 打屁聊天. Harmless small talk; nothing to do with spanking.

en: to chat, to make small talk

example.en: He's great at chatting with customers.

note: Light, sociable chatter; a good salesperson 很會哈拉. Slightly dated but alive.

example.en: I'm on my period and my stomach hurts.

note: Taiwan's polite euphemism; also 那個來 or MC. The mainland says 大姨妈. Context makes the meaning clear.

example.en: He got first place and now he's all cocky.

note: Acting superior. The mainland writes 拽. 跩什麼跩 = "what are you so cocky about?"

example.en: He talks so sleazily that girls steer clear.

note: Borrowed from mainland 油膩 around 2020; now common on Dcard and Threads for try-hard flirty men.

example.zh: 他很愛在大家面前耍寶。
example.en: He loves clowning around in front of everyone.

note: From Taiwanese variety-show culture. Affectionate: the class clown 很愛耍寶.

example.en: I spilled my bubble tea, boo-hoo.

note: Baby-talk doubling (怕怕, 痛痛, 吃飯飯) is a hallmark of Taiwanese cutesy speech (撒嬌). Cute from young women, cloying if overdone.

example.en: She talks in such a whiny-cute voice, I can't stand it.

note: From Taiwanese nai (to act spoiled); written in zhuyin. The stereotyped baby-voice manner; can be praise or mockery.

en: to cram, to hit the books

example.en: I'm going to the library to cram.

note: K is slang for "hit". K書中心 = paid study hall. Student slang for decades; K also = to beat (被K).

example.en: The aunties at the market are all so friendly.

note: Short for 歐巴桑 (Japanese obasan via Taiwanese). Fine when talking about someone; calling a woman 阿桑 to her face can offend, so say 阿姨 or 大姊.

example.en: I've turned into an old auntie.

note: From Japanese obasan via Taiwanese oo-bá-sáng. Suggests a loud, thrifty auntie; often self-mockery. Do not address anyone this way.

example.zh: 隔壁的歐吉桑很愛聊天。
example.en: The old guy next door loves to chat.

note: From Japanese ojisan via Taiwanese oo-jí-sáng. Neutral to slightly comic when talking about a man; to his face use 大哥 or 阿伯.

example.zh: 那個阿兜仔中文講得很好。
example.en: That Westerner speaks really good Chinese.

note: Taiwanese a-tok-á "pointy nose". Not hostile but old-fashioned and a bit othering; you may hear it about yourself from older people. Younger speakers say 外國人.

example.en: Kids should listen and not talk back.

note: Taiwanese gín-á, always pronounced that way. Appears in sayings and affectionate talk (囝仔人 = kids). The example is a proverb every Taiwanese child has heard.

example.en: This line of work is really tough.

note: Taiwanese kan-khóo. Carries sympathy for hardship; 甘苦人 = people who toil for little. Heartfelt and working-class in tone, often said in Taiwanese.

en: what the hell are you doing?

example.zh: 你半夜不睡覺是在衝三小？
example.en: What the hell are you doing up in the middle of the night?

note: Taiwanese tshòng siánn-siâu. Aggressive when aimed at a stranger (a classic street-fight opener); jokey among buddies.

example.en: What? You're getting married?

note: Taiwanese siánn-mih, also written 蝦米. Used for comic surprise inside Mandarin. Harmless; the polite counterpart of 三小.

example.en: Say what? Overtime again tomorrow?

note: Taiwanese siánn-huè (啥貨) spelled by sound. Playful disbelief, common in texting and headlines. Harmless.

example.en: That's no good, think again.

note: Taiwanese án-ne spelled by sound. 安捏喔 = "oh, is that so"; 麥安捏 = "don't be like that". Humorous, folksy flavor in texts and ads.

example.en: Quit it, I'm at work.

note: Taiwanese mài nāu. 麥 (mài) = don't: 麥擱講 = say no more. Light and friendly; also written 賣鬧.

en: to put on an act; to be up to something

example.zh: 你不要在那邊假鬼假怪。
example.en: Stop putting on that act.

note: Taiwanese ké-kuí-ké-kuài. Calls out pretence or sneaky behavior, usually said in Taiwanese. Mild scolding tone.

en: to act recklessly, to do as one pleases

example.en: You can't just wing something like this.

note: Taiwanese oo-pe̍h-lâi. The same 黑白 as in 黑白講 and the food term 黑白切. A parent's or boss's warning.

example.zh: 他開車很鴨霸，都不讓人。
example.en: He drives like a bully and never yields.

note: Taiwanese ah-pà (壓霸). For people who push others around and ignore rules; common in talk about politics.

example.en: Your grandson is so adorable.

note: Taiwanese kóo-tsui. What grandmas say about babies; young people use it for a folksy, affectionate "cute".

example.en: He's an honest sort; he won't cheat you.

note: Taiwanese kóo-ì. Praise for a sincere, unpretentious person, classically the ideal son-in-law. Can hint at "a bit naive".

example.en: The supporters chanted "get elected" together.

note: Taiwanese tòng-suán (當選) spelled by sound. The chant at every election rally; it is all over the news each campaign season.

example.en: Damn, my wallet's gone.

note: Mandarin-character reading of Taiwanese khàu-iau, i.e. the same word as 靠腰. This spelling is mostly an exclamation of dismay. Mild-to-mid vulgarity.

example.en: This place is cheap and the portions are big.

note: Taiwanese sio̍k. Best known in 俗擱大碗 "cheap and generous". Not to be confused with 聳 (sông) "tacky", which is also sometimes written 俗.

example.en: This cafeteria is cheap and gives big portions.

note: Taiwanese sio̍k koh tuā-uánn "cheap and a big bowl too". Standard praise for food stalls and bargains; often written 俗又大碗.

example.en: This flowery shirt is so tacky.

note: Taiwanese sông (倯), pronounced sóng even in Mandarin. 聳擱有力 = "tacky but punchy", now a point of local pride. Rude when aimed at someone's taste.

en: stereotypical local Taiwanese guy (flashy, earthy style)

example.zh: 他以前是染金髮的台客。
example.en: He used to be a bleach-blond local tough-guy type.

note: Originally a slur for unsophisticated Taiwanese men; reclaimed in the 2000s as a style (台客搖滾). The female form is 台妹. Still not a compliment to strangers.

example.en: My grandpa speaks Mandarin with a heavy Taiwanese accent.

note: Mandarin with strong Taiwanese-language features (f becomes h, no retroflexes). Affectionate comic material, but mocking someone's accent can offend.

example.en: Driver, please stop at the next intersection.

note: From Japanese unchan via Taiwanese ùn-tsiàng. A warm, slightly old-school term; as address use 運將大哥 or just 大哥.

example.en: Boss, how much is this?

note: Taiwanese thâu-ke. Used at markets and small shops, usually said in Taiwanese. Friendly and local; 老闆 is the neutral choice.

example.zh: 頭家娘人很好，常常多給。
example.en: The boss lady is so nice, she often gives extra.

note: Taiwanese thâu-ke-niû. Same folksy flavor as 頭家. The Mandarin 老闆娘 (clipped to 闆娘) is more common among the young.

example.zh: 我表哥結婚要在路邊辦桌。
example.en: My cousin is holding his wedding banquet by the roadside.

note: Taiwanese pān-toh. Round tables under a tent, cooked on site by a 總舖師, for weddings, temple feasts and year-end parties. Fading in cities, alive in the south.
