example.en: Hey uncle, have you eaten?

note: Taiwanese tsia̍h-pá--buē (食飽未). A warm hello, not an invitation; the answer is 呷飽了. 呷 is said tsia̍h, never with its Mandarin reading.

en: "good things are worth sharing" (spread the word)

example.en: This place is great; spread the word.

note: Taiwanese tsia̍h hó tàu sio-pò, an old ad slogan that became a proverb. Said when recommending food or a bargain to friends.

example.en: Seafood is best fresh off the boat.

note: Taiwanese siōng tshenn "freshest", fixed in memory by the Taiwan Beer slogan 啥米尚青. 尚 (siōng) = most: 尚讚, 尚好.

example.en: "What do you want to drink?" "Whatever."

note: Taiwanese tshìn-tshái (凊彩) "casually, whatever" sounds like Mandarin 青菜, hence the jokey spelling. Easygoing; same caveats as 隨便.

example.en: Come hang out together when you're free.

note: Taiwanese tàu-tīn, also written 逗陣. 鬥陣的 = buddy, companion. Warm and folksy; common in ads and community events.

en: to back each other up, to have someone's back

example.en: Thank you all for backing me the whole way.

note: Taiwanese sio-thīn. Loyal support among friends, fans or voters; 情義相挺 is the set phrase. 挺你 = "I've got your back".

example.zh: 教你一個省錢的小撇步。
example.en: Let me teach you a little money-saving trick.

note: Taiwanese phiat-pōo. A friendly word for a practical hack; lifestyle shows and blogs love 小撇步.

en: labor-intensive, a lot of trouble to make

example.zh: 這道菜很厚工，要燉六小時。
example.en: This dish is a lot of work; it stews for six hours.

note: Taiwanese kāu-kang, also spelled 搞剛. Often admiring: made the slow way by hand. The internet meme 歸剛欸 is a different word.

en: can't stand it any longer; can't hold back

example.en: It smells too good, I can't hold out.

note: Taiwanese tòng-buē-tiâu (擋袂牢). For heat, hunger, temptation or pressure. Playful, and usually said in Taiwanese.

en: to go crazy, to lose it

example.en: If I keep working overtime I'm going to lose it.

note: Taiwanese khí-siáu (起痟). 肖 (siáu) = crazy: 肖仔 = lunatic, 肖想 = pipe dream. Casual and mildly crude.

example.en: Kids mustn't tell lies.

note: Taiwanese pe̍h-tsha̍t. Folksy and a little childlike; 白賊七 is a folk-tale liar. Otherwise Mandarin uses 說謊.

en: to lose face, to embarrass oneself

example.zh: 在大家面前跌倒，超漏氣。
example.en: Falling over in front of everyone was so embarrassing.

note: Taiwanese làu-khuì "leak air". 給我漏氣 = make me lose face. Slightly older-generation flavor; 丟臉 is the neutral word.

en: to slip up, to botch it

example.en: The host kept slipping up today.

note: Taiwanese thut-tshuê. Blunders on stage or at work; interchangeable with 出包 but more colorful.

en: to come up empty (lottery, fishing, a bet)

example.en: No winning receipt numbers again this round.

note: Taiwanese kòng-ku. The standard word for not winning the lottery or the bimonthly receipt lottery, and for a fruitless fishing trip.

example.zh: 這支舊手機已經沒路用了。
example.en: This old phone is no use anymore.

note: Taiwanese bô-lōo-īng. About a person it is a harsh family-style scolding (沒路用的人); about things it is neutral.

example.en: The way he talks rubs everyone the wrong way.

note: Taiwanese kòo-lâng-uàn. Describes people whose manner invites dislike. Blunt but not vulgar.

example.en: I'm hopeless at basketball.

note: Taiwanese bah-kha. For sports, games and drinking. Teasing or self-deprecating; mild.

example.en: Hiding at the first sign of trouble. What a wimp.

note: Taiwanese nńg-kha-hê "soft-legged shrimp". Scornful but printable; common in political commentary.

example.zh: 他們講太快，我都鴨子聽雷。
example.en: They talk so fast I can't follow a thing.

note: Taiwanese ah-á thiann luî "a duck hearing thunder". Handy self-deprecation for a learner.

example.en: You're talking too fast, I can't follow.

note: Taiwanese thiann-bô, said in Taiwanese; informally also written 聽嘸. A friendly way to admit you are lost.

example.en: Hello everyone, I'm new here.

note: Taiwanese lí-hó spelled by sound. A playful greeting in texts and from hosts; native Taiwanese speakers more often greet with 呷飽沒.

example.en: Yours truly is in a bad mood today.

note: Taiwanese lín-pē (恁爸). Swaggering self-reference like mainland 老子. Comic among male friends, belligerent toward others.

example.en: Lose five kilos in three days? Who are you kidding.

note: Taiwanese phiàn-siáu (騙痟), often 騙肖欸. Blunt disbelief; mildly crude because of siáu. Friends only.

en: to talk nonsense, to joke around

example.zh: 他們幾個整晚都在練肖話。
example.en: Those guys spent the whole night talking nonsense.

note: Taiwanese liān-siáu-uē (練痟話). Cheerful rubbish talk, cruder in feel than 喇賽. Close to the newer Mandarin 講幹話.

example.zh: 阿公喜歡在廟口跟人抬槓。
example.en: Grandpa likes to sit outside the temple and chat with people.

note: In Taiwan, under the influence of Taiwanese thâi-kòng, it mostly means casual chatting; mainland 抬杠 means arguing for the sake of it. A classic false friend.

example.zh: 薪水沒漲，大家都在該該叫。
example.en: No raise, and everyone's whining.

note: Taiwanese kainn-kainn-kiò, a yelping sound. Common on PTT and in headlines; slightly mocking toward the complainers. Close cousin: 哀哀叫.

example.en: His English is amazingly good.

note: Taiwanese siah-siah-kiò. Follows a verb or 強到. Upbeat and a little old-fashioned; an ad-copy favorite.

example.en: Business at the night market is booming.

note: Taiwanese tshiâng-tshiâng-kún "boiling hard". For crowds, sales and atmospheres. A news and marketing staple.

en: lavish, generous (of a spread of food)

example.zh: 今天晚餐也太澎湃了吧。
example.en: Tonight's dinner is quite the feast.

note: Taiwanese phong-phài (豐沛). In Taiwan 澎湃 often describes a table loaded with food, besides the standard sense "surging".

example.zh: 住這一區的都是好野人。
example.en: Everyone living in this area is loaded.

note: Taiwanese hó-gia̍h-lâng (好額人) spelled by sound. Light-hearted envy; common in news headlines.

example.zh: 少年仔，幫我搬一下好嗎？
example.en: Young man, could you give me a hand moving this?

note: Taiwanese siàu-liân-á (also 少年欸, siàu-liân-ê). How older men and vendors address a young guy. You answer to it; you do not say it to elders.

example.zh: 車站有很多放假的阿兵哥。
example.en: There are lots of soldiers on leave at the station.

note: Taiwanese a-ping-ko. An affectionate everyday term, tied to Taiwan's conscription culture (當兵).

en: to cast moon blocks to ask the gods

example.en: He went to the temple to cast moon blocks about his career.

note: Usually said in Taiwanese: pua̍h-pue. One flat and one round side up is 聖筊 (a yes). People also 擲筊 half-jokingly to make decisions.

example.en: Come on, everybody, bottoms up!

note: Taiwanese hōo ta--lah "let it be dry". The rowdy toast at 熱炒 restaurants and banquets. Among friends; to elders say 我敬你.

example.zh: 點這道就知道你是巷仔內的。
example.en: Ordering this dish shows you're in the know.

note: Taiwanese hāng-á-lāi "inside the alley". An insider with real local knowledge; 巷仔內美食 = spots only locals know.

en: to like, to take a fancy to

example.zh: 這件我很甲意，幫我包起來。
example.en: I really like this one; wrap it up for me.

note: Taiwanese kah-ì (佮意), also spelled 尬意. Folksy; used jokingly in Mandarin for things or people that catch your eye.

example.zh: 店員還幫我撐傘，揪感心。
example.en: The clerk even held an umbrella for me. So thoughtful.

note: Taiwanese tsiok kám-sim (足感心). A media and social-post favorite for small kind acts; 揪 here just spells tsiok "very".

example.en: I'm not in a great mood today.

note: From Japanese kimochi via Taiwanese khi-móo-tsih. Usually 奇檬子很好 or 奇檬子不爽. Older, working-class flavor; young people use it for humor.

example.en: Have you gone loopy?

note: From Japanese shōto "short circuit" via Taiwanese. Gentle teasing with a 1990s flavor. Related: 阿達 (from 阿達馬 "head", Japanese atama).

example.en: The service here is first-rate.

note: From Japanese ichiban via Taiwanese, with characters chosen to mean "first-class great". Cheerful and slightly retro.

example.zh: 半夜有人在大度路尬車。
example.en: People were street-racing on Dadu Road in the middle of the night.

note: 尬 spells Taiwanese kà "to compete": 尬車, 尬舞 (dance battle), 尬酒. Separate from the newer 很尬 "awkward".

en: to plunge in, to go all in

example.en: Now that it's decided, just go all in.

note: Taiwanese liâu--lo̍h-khì "wade right in". A rallying phrase for committing to a hard task; common in politics and startups.

example.zh: 小孩想睡的時候都很番。
example.en: Kids get impossible when they're sleepy.

note: Taiwanese huan. Widely used, but 番 was a derogatory word for indigenous peoples, so many now avoid it. Safer: 很盧, 不講理.

example.en: I've been a single loser for thirty years.

note: From 魯蛇 (loser). On PTT 小魯 or 魯弟 is a humble "I"; 脫魯 = finally get a partner. Rare in speech; you will mostly read it.

en: to downvote, to boo (a PTT post)

example.en: His post got booed into oblivion.

note: The opposite of 推; 噓爆 = buried in boos. Outside PTT, 被噓 means being jeered at. Also the shushing sound "shh".

example.zh: 樓主加油，我們都支持你。
example.en: Hang in there, OP, we're all behind you.

note: Forum term shared with the mainland; common on Dcard, Bahamut and Mobile01, while PTT prefers 原po. 樓上 = the commenter above.

example.zh: 情人節單身狗只能在家追劇。
example.en: On Valentine's Day us singles can only stay home and binge shows.

note: Mainland-origin term fully adopted in Taiwan. Use it about yourself; calling someone else one is a bit mean.

example.en: This ramen place is really good.

note: Using 可以 as an adjective became a youth fad around 2017. Approving, slightly ironic. Still common in food posts.

example.zh: 我就爛，報告還沒開始寫。
example.en: I just suck. I haven't even started the report.

note: A 2019 Dcard-born meme; the original line is 啊我就爛. Shrugs off criticism by owning it. Funny among friends, obnoxious to a teacher or boss.

en: "what a hassle!"; for crying out loud

example.en: Have to line up all over again. What a hassle.

note: Taiwanese kui-kang "the whole day" + 欸, popularized by a streamer around 2021–2022. Exasperation at something tiresome. Young, male-leaning; said in Taiwanese.

example.zh: 我們教官超派，沒人敢遲到。
example.en: Our drill officer is super fierce; nobody dares be late.

note: 派 spells Taiwanese pháinn (歹) "fierce, bad". A 2023 viral clip of a schoolkid made 超派 and 很派 the buzzwords of the year. Playful.

example.zh: 我有點社恐，不太敢打電話。
example.en: I'm a bit socially anxious; phone calls make me nervous.

note: Short for 社交恐懼. A mainland-origin clipping now normal among Taiwanese under 35, used loosely for "shy, awkward".

example.en: I diet Buddha-style: whatever happens, happens.

note: From Japan via the mainland around 2017–2018. 佛系 + noun: 佛系員工, 佛系追星. Mildly humorous and still in use.

en: to "lie flat": opt out of the rat race

example.zh: 房價這麼高，乾脆躺平算了。
example.en: With housing prices this high, might as well just lie flat.

note: A 2021 mainland buzzword, understood and used in Taiwan, often about housing and low pay. Some speakers avoid mainland slang (called 支語), so read the room.

en: to not even open someone's messages

example.zh: 我傳了三則訊息，她不讀不回。
example.en: I sent three messages and she hasn't even opened them.

note: A step colder than 已讀不回: the message stays unread. It usually means you are being ghosted.

example.zh: 看影評之前要小心劇透。
example.en: Watch out for spoilers before reading reviews.

note: Shared with the mainland and common in media headlines; in conversation Taiwanese more often say 爆雷 or 有雷.

en: to ignore, to treat as invisible; fake (friendship)

example.zh: 我講話你都不理，當我塑膠？
example.en: You ignore everything I say. Am I invisible to you?

note: 當我塑膠 "treat me like plastic" came from game streamers around 2017. 塑膠姊妹 (fake besties) follows mainland 塑料姐妹. Said sù jiāo in Taiwan.

example.en: Some hooligans downstairs were making noise in the middle of the night.

note: Pun on 八家將 (temple procession troupes), read 八加九. Stereotype: modified scooters, tattoos, street fights. Derogatory; never say it within earshot.

example.en: Are you an idiot? How do you get lost here?

note: 87 reads like 北七 (Taiwanese pe̍h-tshi "idiot"). 87分不能再高了 is the extended meme. A friendly insult in texting.

example.en: Heh. Whatever makes you happy.

note: Zhuyin initials of 呵呵 or 哈哈. Usually reads as cold or sarcastic, not amused. Genuine laughter is 哈哈哈, XD or 笑死.

example.en: Hehe, I guessed right, didn't I.

note: Zhuyin for a snicker (also written 顆顆). Mischievous or smug. Old-school BBS flavor that survives in chats.

en: "zhuyin writing": replacing characters with bopomofo letters

example.zh: 拜託不要用注音文，很難看懂。
example.en: Please don't write in zhuyin shorthand; it's hard to read.

note: Typing only the first zhuyin symbol (ㄉ, ㄇ, ㄅ, ㄋ) of a word. Associated with teens of the 2000s. Light use is playful; heavy use annoys people.

example.en: You're the greatest. Aren't you just wonderful.

note: From the 2014 meme 啊不就好棒棒. Baby-talk praise used sarcastically at show-offs. Sincere use is only for small children.

example.zh: 安安，請問這個還有在賣嗎？
example.en: Hi there, is this still for sale?

note: From 午安, 晚安. An early-2000s chatroom greeting (安安你好，幾歲住哪) that people still use half-ironically to open a message.

en: to kill the conversation (leave nothing to reply to)

example.zh: 我傳了一長串，他只回喔，被句點。
example.en: I sent a long message and he just replied "oh". Conversation killed.

note: "Full stop" as a verb. 句點王 = someone whose replies end every chat. The dreaded replies: 喔, 是喔, 哈哈, 嗯嗯.

example.zh: 那個奧客被鄉民肉搜出來。
example.en: Netizens tracked down who that nightmare customer was.

note: Short for 人肉搜索. A staple of Taiwanese online outrage cycles; also used for looking someone up before a date.

example.zh: 這篇文章明顯在帶風向。
example.en: This post is obviously trying to steer opinion.

note: 風向 = the direction comments are blowing. PTT-born; the mainland says 带节奏. Common in political arguments.

example.zh: 我的同溫層都在討論這件事。
example.en: Everyone in my bubble is talking about this.

note: People who think like you on social media. 同溫層太厚 = living in a bubble. Standard vocabulary in election season.

example.zh: 我只是無聊發廢文而已。
example.en: I was just bored and shitposting.

note: 發廢文 is a proud pastime on PTT and Dcard. Calling someone else's post 廢文 is an insult. Mainland: 水帖.

example.zh: 小心前面那輛車，可能是三寶。
example.en: Watch out for that car ahead; could be a terrible driver.

note: From 馬路三寶, a mid-2010s PTT stereotype blaming women, the elderly and older women for bad driving. Now any reckless road user. Sexist and ageist in origin.

example.en: No overtime pay again. Typical entitled boss.

note: A boss "spoiled rotten" by compliant workers. A PTT-born term in debates over low pay and long hours.

example.zh: 修但幾勒，你剛剛說什麼？
example.en: Hold on a sec, what did you just say?

note: Taiwanese sió-tán--tsi̍t-ē (稍等一下) spelled by sound. A meme spelling since about 2019, used to stop someone mid-flow. Playful.

example.zh: 我只有五百，要麻煩你找零。
example.en: I only have a five hundred; I'll need change, sorry.

note: Cash is still widely used. The cashier's formula: 收您一千，找您兩百. 不用找了 = keep the change.

example.en: Good afternoon, everyone.

note: More formal than 早安: announcements, customer service, older people's LINE messages. Friends would just say 嗨.

example.en: That's enough from you two.

note: A mock-stern warning, often said laughing when friends tease or flirt too much. With a cold tone it is a real warning.

en: "drink as you like" (no need to finish the glass)

example.en: I'll drain mine; you drink what you like.

note: The gracious counterpart to 乾杯 at banquets. 我乾杯你隨意 shows respect to the other person.

en: "take care" (said to a departing guest or customer)

example.en: Thank you for coming, take care.

note: Said by hosts and shopkeepers, never by the one leaving. Sounds a bit traditional; younger staff just say 謝謝.

en: "can you make it a bit cheaper?"

example.zh: 老闆，買兩個算便宜一點啦。
example.en: Boss, I'm buying two; give me a better price.

note: A bargaining formula for markets and independent stalls, not chain stores. Keep smiling; 啦 helps. Full tones: pián yí.

example.en: He always orders full sugar. So sweet.

note: Also called 正常甜. Very sweet by most people's standards; ordering it earns jokes about diabetes.

example.en: I'd like big pearls in my milk tea.

note: 波霸 was 1980s slang for a busty woman, jokingly applied to big pearls. 波霸奶茶 is the source of English "boba".

example.en: The pork in this place's gua bao is really fatty.

note: From Taiwanese kuah-pau; 刈 is read guà here. A steamed bun with braised pork, pickled greens, peanut powder and cilantro.

example.zh: 夏天就是要來一碗剉冰。
example.en: Summer calls for a bowl of shaved ice.

note: From Taiwanese tshuah-ping; also written 刨冰. Pick three or four toppings (配料): red beans, taro balls, pudding. 雪花冰 is the finer, milky kind.

en: moreish; you can't stop eating it

example.en: These chips are really moreish.

note: From Taiwanese suà-tshuì. For snacks and dishes that keep you reaching for more. A favorite word in food reviews.

example.en: Can I get a refill on the black tea?

note: Free refills (免費續杯) exist at some breakfast shops and fast-food chains. Ask first.

example.zh: 我第一次喝鹹豆漿就愛上了。
example.en: I fell in love with savory soy milk the first time I tried it.

note: Hot soy milk curdled with vinegar, topped with dried shrimp, pickles and fried dough. A soy-milk-shop classic alongside 燒餅油條.

example.zh: 老闆，蛋餅加一杯大冰奶。
example.en: Boss, an egg crepe and a large iced milk tea.

note: Breakfast-shop shorthand for 大杯冰奶茶. Folk wisdom says it sends you straight to the bathroom.

example.zh: 逢甲夜市的大腸包小腸很有名。
example.en: The sausage-in-rice-sausage at Fengjia Night Market is famous.

note: A grilled pork sausage inside a split sticky-rice sausage, with garlic and pickles. A night-market icon.

example.zh: 我買了兩個奶油車輪餅。
example.en: I bought two custard wheel cakes.

note: Also 紅豆餅. From Japanese imagawayaki. Standard fillings: red bean, custard, shredded radish.

example.en: Night-market sweet potato balls are fragrant and chewy.

note: A hollow, chewy night-market snack. 地瓜 is the Taiwan word for sweet potato (mainland 红薯) and a symbol of Taiwan itself.

example.zh: 冬天去超商買關東煮最棒。
example.en: Buying oden at the convenience store in winter is the best.

note: From Japanese. Self-service at convenience stores. The Taiwanese-language cousin is 黑輪 (oo-lián).

example.zh: 冬天晚上來一鍋薑母鴨最棒。
example.en: A pot of ginger duck stew on a winter night is the best.

note: A winter tonic (進補) hot pot with rice wine, eaten on low stools at roadside shops. Its cousins are 羊肉爐 and 麻油雞.

en: "do you want it cut?" (fried chicken stall question)

example.en: The vendor asked me, "Want your cutlet cut?"

note: The ritual 雞排 questions are 要切嗎？要辣嗎？ Purists say 不切 keeps it juicy. Answer 要 or 不用.

example.zh: 自備環保杯可以折五元。
example.en: Bring your own cup and you get five NT off.

note: Bringing your own cup earns a discount at chain shops. Also 環保筷, 環保袋. 自備 = bring your own.

example.en: There's something good for dinner tonight.

note: From Taiwanese hó-liāu, usually as 吃好料的. A small splurge, not necessarily fancy.

en: to fill up cheaply (quantity over quality)

example.zh: 學生時代都只是吃粗飽。
example.en: Back in my student days I just filled up cheaply.

note: From Taiwanese tsia̍h-tshoo-pá. Eating only to be full, typically big portions of carbs. Mildly self-deprecating.

example.zh: 這條街有很多銅板美食。
example.en: This street has lots of cheap eats.

note: 銅板 = coins: snacks under about NT$50. A stock phrase of food shows and blogs, though inflation is eroding it.

en: food worth queuing for; famous-queue eatery

example.zh: 這家是有名的排隊美食。
example.en: This place is a famous queue-up spot.

note: Taiwanese will join a long line on principle. Also 排隊名店. Whether it was worth the wait is a favorite topic.

example.zh: 點一碗麵再加一盤黑白切。
example.en: Order a bowl of noodles plus a plate of mixed sliced sides.

note: Taiwanese oo-pe̍h-tshiat "randomly sliced": pork offal, tofu and the like, sliced to order at noodle stalls. Point, or let the owner choose.

example.zh: 他懷疑老婆在外面有小王。
example.en: He suspects his wife has another man.

note: The male counterpart of 小三, a Taiwan coinage. Common in gossip news: 人妻與小王.

example.en: I'm spending the weekend with my other half.

note: From PTT: couples "flash" singles, so one's partner is a 閃光. Gender-neutral and playful; peaked in the 2010s. Often 我家閃光.

example.en: I don't want to keep loving someone who doesn't love me back.

note: Unlike 暗戀, the other person may know and simply not feel the same.

en: to reject a suitor (hand out a "nice-guy card")

example.en: She flat-out rejected him yesterday.

note: The giver's side of 好人卡. 被發卡 = be turned down. Light, self-mocking register.

example.zh: 我今年三十歲，還是母胎單身。
example.en: I'm thirty this year and have never dated anyone.

note: From Korean motae solo. Self-deprecating. Abbreviated 母單.

example.zh: 不要想了，人家已經死會了。
example.en: Forget it, she's already taken.

note: From rotating credit clubs (標會): a 死會 member has already drawn the pot. 活會 = still available. Slightly old-school, widely understood.

example.en: Baby, are you off work yet?

note: Sound-loan of "baby". Cutesy couple talk, like 寶貝, 寶寶, 哈尼 (honey). Friends will tease you for it.

en: to be smitten with, to fall for at first sight

example.en: I was smitten with her at first sight.

note: From Taiwanese sannh--tio̍h. Sudden, strong attraction. Casual; common in variety-show talk.

example.zh: 你們兩個看起來很速配。
example.en: You two look like a great match.

note: Taiwanese sù-phuè, popularized by the 1990s dating show 非常男女. A warm compliment to couples.

example.en: He loves flirting with the girls in the shop.

note: From Taiwanese khui. 虧妹 = chat up girls with teasing banter; 虧我 = make fun of me. Playful, sometimes annoying.

example.en: He's really smooth at flirting with girls.

note: Mainland-origin (2016), now standard among young Taiwanese alongside the native 把妹. 撩 = flirt, tease: 很會撩.

en: player (someone who dates around for fun)

example.zh: 他是出名的玩咖，不要當真。
example.en: He's a notorious player; don't take him seriously.

note: 咖 from Taiwanese kha "player, type". Suggests nightlife and no commitment. A native Taiwan term; mainland youth say 海王.

example.zh: 她有公主病，什麼都要人伺候。
example.en: She's got princess syndrome and expects to be waited on.

note: Said of women who expect pampering. Common but gendered and unkind; the male version is 王子病.

example.zh: 分手後他變成恐怖情人。
example.en: After the breakup he turned into a scary, stalking ex.

note: A Taiwanese media term for partners who stalk, threaten or turn violent, especially after a breakup.

example.zh: 他們只是砲友，不是情侶。
example.en: They're just friends with benefits, not a couple.

note: Crude but widely used in dating talk. 約砲 = hook up. Not for polite company.

example.zh: 這個月我收到三張紅色炸彈。
example.en: I got three wedding invitations this month.

note: Each invitation obliges a red envelope of cash (包紅包), hence "bomb". Amounts follow strict etiquette; avoid any figure with a 4.

example.en: I actually wanted to go too, you know.

note: Tacked on to sound soft or mildly regretful; big in the 2000s BBS and MSN era. Still heard from people in their 30s and 40s, mostly ironic now.

example.en: He's a winner: car, apartment, the works.

note: Transliteration of "winner", PTT's pair to 魯蛇. Usually envious sarcasm. Also 人生勝利組. Seen in text more than heard in speech.

example.en: Going clubbing dressed like that? So uncool.

note: Very 1990s; use it ironically or expect a laugh. The same goes for 遜斃了.

example.en: This doggy is sooo cute.

note: Mimics Taiwan-accented Mandarin, in which 很 comes out like 粉. A late-1990s–2000s cutesy spelling that now reads as retro or mock-cute. Recognize it; do not use it seriously.

example.en: This charm is so kawaii.

note: From Japanese kawaii. Peaked in the 1990s–2000s Japan craze; now used with deliberate cutesiness.

en: to be crazy about Japanese culture

example.en: She's been a Japanophile since she was little.

note: Coined in 1990s Taiwan (哈 from Taiwanese hah "to crave"); also 哈韓. Dated: now people just say 很愛日本.

en: rich sucker; man who splurges on women

example.en: She's just using him as a sugar daddy.

note: 1980s–90s slang (釣凱子 = hunt for a rich sucker). Middle-aged flavor; young people say 盤子 or 工具人.

example.en: You're asking me? I have no idea either.

note: Taiwanese m̄ tsai-iánn spelled with funny characters ("don't slaughter the sheep"). An old pun everyone knows; dad-joke territory.

en: placeholder comment to follow a thread

example.en: This thread is great; leaving a comment to follow it.

note: Short for 卡位 "claim a spot". A one-character comment on Dcard or Facebook so that you get notified of updates. Purely written.

example.zh: 又是閃文，我要戴墨鏡了。
example.en: Another couple post. Time to put on my sunglasses.

note: Posts so sweet they "blind" single readers (閃 = flash). Singles reply 墨鏡 (sunglasses) or 可惡. PTT-era humor, still understood.

example.zh: 這隻貓可愛到不要不要的。
example.en: This cat is cute like crazy.

note: A 2015 fad from mainland variety shows, used as …到不要不要的. Sounds dated now; mostly ironic.

example.zh: 等不到的公車，像極了愛情。
example.en: A bus that never comes. Just like love.

note: A 2020 meme: write any mundane sentence, then add 像極了愛情 to turn it into "poetry". Faded, but everyone recognizes it.

example.zh: 明天要出國了，哇酷哇酷！
example.en: I'm going abroad tomorrow. So exciting!

note: From Anya's catchphrase "waku waku" in the anime SPY×FAMILY, a 2022–2023 fad. Cute and already fading.

example.zh: 明天考試我都沒念，芭比Q了。
example.en: I haven't studied at all for tomorrow's exam. I'm toast.

note: From a 2021 mainland Douyin clip: barbecue = burnt = finished. Had a moment in Taiwan in 2022; now dated, and some dislike it as imported slang.

example.zh: 補習班越開越多，根本是內卷。
example.en: More and more cram schools. It's pure involution.

note: A 2020 mainland buzzword. Younger Taiwanese understand it and media use it, but it marks you as a consumer of mainland content.

en: "that's just how awesome it is" (就是狂)

example.en: Going to work in a typhoon like nothing's wrong. Just that hardcore.

note: Number pun: 94 = 就是. A 2016 buzzword boosted by a rap song. Dated now; used for nostalgic or ironic effect.

example.en: The one who took my pudding... is it you?

note: A number-letter pun from around 2017, usually a mock-accusing question. A period piece of Taiwanese meme culture.

example.en: You stood me up again. Me so mad.

note: Sound-play on 生氣氣 from around 2016. Pure cutesy texting; dated and used ironically now.

example.en: This is my new phone.

note: The best-known 注音文 substitution: ㄉ = 的. Meant to look cute; many people find it childish, and PTT has long banned it.

example.en: I'm off to shower, bye-bye.

note: Initials of 掰掰. MSN and early-2000s chat flavor; mainland chat used 88 the same way.

example.zh: 在電梯裡放屁被聽到，好囧。
example.en: Someone heard me fart in the elevator. So awkward.

note: An obscure character revived around 2008 because it looks like a dismayed face. Dated but understood; 好囧 = so embarrassing.

en: "so shocked I'm biting my hand" (cutesy; dated)

example.zh: 看到帳單我嚇到吃手手。
example.en: When I saw the bill I was shocked silly.

note: A 2016 meme from a picture of a startled cartoon creature. Media headlines overused it; now a nostalgia item.

en: cross-cultural romance (Taiwanese dating foreigners; PTT term)

example.en: This thread is fighting over cross-cultural romance again.

note: A PTT abbreviation, mostly used disparagingly about local women dating Western men. Worth recognizing; using it yourself invites trouble.
